events/treaty-of-paris-1898.title: Treaty of Paris (1898)
events/treaty-of-paris-1898.content:
Treaty of Paris (1898)
The Treaty of Paris of 1898 formally concluded the spanish-american-war between the United States and Spain. Signed on December 10, 1898, the treaty dismantled Spain’s four-century-old empire in the Americas and the Pacific, ceding Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippine Islands to the United States and transferring Cuba under temporary American military guardianship. The acquisition of an Asian archipelago of over seven million inhabitants transformed American foreign policy and precipitated an intense domestic constitutional debate over imperialism.
The Paris Negotiations
In September 1898, President william-mckinley appointed five peace commissioners: former Secretary of State William R. Day as chairman, Republican Senators Cushman K. Davis and William P. Frye, Democratic Senator George Gray, and Whitelaw Reid, editor of the New York Tribune. The Spanish commission was headed by Don Eugenio Montero Ríos, President of the Spanish Senate. The sessions opened in Paris on October 1, 1898.
The commissioners readily settled the status of the West Indies. Spain relinquished all claim of sovereignty over Cuba without the assumption of the Cuban public debt by either the United States or the newly liberated island, and ceded Puerto Rico and Guam to the United States as indemnification for war expenses.
The central battleground was the disposition of the Philippine Islands. McKinley’s initial instructions demanded only a coaling and naval station or the island of Luzon. However, reports from General Merritt, Admiral Dewey, and commercial representatives argued that dividing the archipelago was strategically and commercially impracticable. Furthermore, British diplomatic encouragement and the hostile maneuvers of a German naval squadron in Manila Bay under Vice Admiral von Diederichs indicated that if the United States withdrew, European rivalries or Japanese expansion would swiftly partition the islands. Concluding that the United States could not return the islands to Spain, abandon them to commercial rivals, or leave them to anarchy, McKinley instructed the commission in late October to demand the entire archipelago. To soften the blow to Spanish pride and settle outstanding infrastructure claims, the American commissioners offered $20,000,000, which the Spanish government reluctantly accepted on November 28. The treaty was signed on December 10, 1898.
The Senate Ratification Struggle
The submission of the treaty to the United States Senate ignited one of the fiercest foreign policy debates in American history. The treaty was challenged by the anti-imperialist-movement, led in the Senate by George F. Hoar of Massachusetts and George G. Vest of Missouri. Opponents argued that acquiring distant, non-contiguous territories inhabited by peoples of different races and cultures without their consent violated the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, requiring an imperial standing army and entangling the republic in Asiatic balance-of-power rivalries.
The administration countered that the United States had assumed a moral obligation of tutelage to pacify, uplift, and prepare the inhabitants for self-government, while securing a vital commercial base for the burgeoning open-door-policy trade in China. The deadlock was broken by William Jennings Bryan, the 1896 Democratic presidential nominee, who traveled to Washington and advised Democratic senators to vote for the treaty. Bryan reasoned that concluding the treaty would officially end the war with Spain, prevent an increase in the standing army, and allow the American people to repudiate colonial imperialism in the upcoming election-of-1900.
On February 4, 1899, two days before the Senate vote, armed clashes erupted on the outskirts of Manila between American troops and Filipino nationalists under Emilio Aguinaldo. News of the outbreak rallied patriotic sentiment in Washington. On February 6, 1899, the Senate ratified the treaty by a vote of 57 to 27—securing the requisite two-thirds majority by a margin of a single vote. Ten Democrats and three Populists voted with the Republican majority. Spain ratified the pact on March 19, and ratifications were exchanged on April 11, 1899, inaugurating both American territorial empire and the bloody guerrilla conflict governed by philippine-policy.

United States 1866–1919 Wiki
A narrative-research knowledge base on American history from Reconstruction after the Civil War through the end of the First World War era — constitutional reconstruction, federal and state politics, industrial capitalism, immigration and urbanization, westward expansion, labor and agrarian movements, Progressive reform, overseas empire, and wartime mobilization through 1919.
Total pages: 70
What follows is the map of the wiki — people, events, and concepts — then the source library on which every claim rests. Entity, event, and concept pages are built from those sources under a contemporary lens, without modern editorial framing.
Entities
Reconstruction executives

andrew-johnson — Seventeenth President: succession after Lincoln, presidential Reconstruction, breach with Congress, impeachment
grant-administration-and-reconstruction — Soldier-President: Stanton crisis path, Fifteenth Amendment, Southern restoration, two terms to 1876
hayes-administration — Seated after disputed 1876; reconciliation policy and close of federal Reconstruction phase

Gilded Age, imperial, and progressive executives

william-mckinley — Twenty-fifth President: gold standard victory of 1896, Spanish-American War, overseas empire, Buffalo reciprocity address, assassination
theodore-roosevelt — Square Deal, trust regulation, New Imperialism hinge, Bull Moose revolt
woodrow-wilson — New Freedom, neutrality and war, Fourteen Points, League fight

Industrial and financial titans

j-p-morgan-sr — Wall Street banker, syndicate organizer, railroad consolidator, 1895 gold rescue, U.S. Steel, Panic of 1907
john-d-rockefeller-sr — Founder of Standard Oil, pioneer of the industrial trust, horizontal and vertical integration, mass scientific philanthropy
andrew-carnegie — Scottish immigrant, master of Carnegie Steel, cost-accounting, Bessemer mass production, Gospel of Wealth
charles-a-lindbergh-sr — Insurgent Minnesota congressman, agrarian prosecutor of the Money Trust, Pujo resolution, anti-war critic

Corporate and banking institutions

house-of-morgan — Merchant banking partnership at 23 Wall Street; railroad reorganization, industrial consolidation, 1907 rescue, Allied purchasing
standard-oil-company — Premier industrial combination; Cleveland refining, pipelines, 26 Broadway, rebates, 1911 Supreme Court dissolution
carnegie-steel-company — Pittsburgh manufacturing partnership; Edgar Thomson works, Frick, vertical integration, Homestead, core of U.S. Steel

Events
Reconstruction settlement

reconstruction-acts — 1867 military districts, conventions, suffrage as condition of readmission
impeachment-of-andrew-johnson — Tenure crisis, House articles, Senate acquittal 1868
disputed-election-of-1876 — Contested returns; Hayes seated; bargain ending enforcement regime

Realignment, empire, and diplomacy

election-of-1896 — Sound money against free silver; realignment establishing Republican ascendancy
spanish-american-war — Swift defeat of Spain in Cuba, Puerto Rico, and Philippines; emergence of overseas power
treaty-of-paris-1898 — Cession of Puerto Rico, Guam, and Philippines for $20,000,000; Senate ratification battle
election-of-1900 — McKinley and Roosevelt defeat Bryan on the “full dinner pail” and imperialism
assassination-of-william-mckinley — Buffalo Pan-American shooting by Czolgosz; death and succession of Theodore Roosevelt
panama-canal-and-isthmian-diplomacy — Hay-Pauncefote to Goethals; isthmian hinge of New Imperialism
election-of-1912 — Taft–Roosevelt–Wilson; Progressive schism elects a Democrat
league-of-nations-debate — Covenant, Lodge reservations, Senate rejection, Wilson’s collapse

Panics, corporate mergers, and labor conflict

panic-of-1893 — Railroad insolvencies, European gold flight, unemployment, Coxey’s army, Pullman strike, silver repeal
gold-standard-crisis-of-1895 — Depletion of Treasury gold reserve, Morgan-Rothschild bond syndicate contract, populist backlash
homestead-strike — 1892 armed labor battle at Carnegie mill, Pinkertons, state militia, destruction of steel unionism
formation-of-united-states-steel — 1901 Morgan buyout of Carnegie Steel; first billion-dollar corporation consolidating steel trade
panic-of-1907 — Knickerbocker Trust collapse, Morgan’s library rescue pools, Tennessee Coal & Iron buyout, path to Federal Reserve
ludlow-massacre — 1914 Colorado coal strike fire, Rockefeller family crisis, Ivy Lee PR, and pioneering corporate welfare capitalism

Concepts
Constitution and party

thirteenth-amendment — Abolition as war result; federative system claimed still intact
fourteenth-amendment — Citizenship and representation; first condition of readmission
fifteenth-amendment — National bar on racial denial of the ballot
tenure-of-office-act — Senate curb on removals; hinge of the impeachment
congressional-reconstruction — Congress fixes terms of Southern return
republican-party-after-the-civil-war — Union-victory party become Reconstruction majority
popular-memory-of-reconstruction — Late-century schoolbook plot of Johnson–Grant–Hayes

Empire, commerce, and anti-imperialism

new-imperialism — Overseas power after Spain; Open Door and Caribbean
anti-imperialist-movement — League resistance against Philippine annexation, standing armies, and colonial despotism
philippine-policy — Military pacification of Aguinaldo, Schurman and Taft commissions, insular civil government
open-door-policy — Hay circulars, Boxer Rebellion relief, and defense of Chinese territorial integrity
teller-and-platt-amendments — Non-annexation pledge of 1898 and terms of Cuban protectorate of 1901
reciprocity-and-international-trade — Shift from insular protection toward reciprocal trade treaties to absorb industrial surplus

Finance, monopoly, and philanthropy

standard-oil-trust — Dodd’s 1882 legal device unifying multistate properties under nine trustees; catalyst for Sherman Antitrust Act
money-trust — Progressive critique of concentrated banking power; Pujo Committee exposure of $22 billion in interlocking directorates
gospel-of-wealth — Carnegie’s doctrine that surplus wealth is a sacred trust to be administered during life; library and educational benefactions
rockefeller-philanthropy — Gates’s scientific wholesale giving; University of Chicago, medical research, General Education Board, Rockefeller Foundation
banking-reform-and-the-federal-reserve-act — 1913 Glass-Owen legislation ending currency inelasticity and reserve-pyramiding via twelve regional banks

Progressivism and war

progressive-era — Regulation, exposure, insurgency, New Freedom
progressive-party — Bull Moose of 1912; Roosevelt–Johnson ticket
world-war-i-mobilization — Selective Service, boards, finance, home front 1917–18
fourteen-points — Wilson’s war aims and League as coping-stone

Sources
The foundation of the wiki. Source pages summarize the primary and secondary texts used throughout.

Paxson’s revised and enlarged synthesis of United States history from the end of the Civil War through the 1920s, emphasizing Reconstruction, industrial society, the end of the frontier, party politics, imperial expansion, Progressive reform, Wilson, World War I, peace, and postwar normalcy. Read source page

Blaine’s first volume on the prelude to the political revolution of 1860, the Civil War, Lincoln’s administration, wartime Congress, finance, emancipation, and the political setting that led into Reconstruction. Read source page
blaine-twenty-years-of-congress-volume-2 — [source] Twenty Years of Congress, Volume II (Blaine, 1886) — James G. Blaine’s second volume on Reconstruction, Andrew Johnson, congressional Republicans, constitutional amendments, impeachment, Southern readmission, civil rights, Grant-era politics, and the movement from Lincoln toward Garfield. Read source page
ridpath-united-states-a-history — [source] United States: A History (Ridpath, 1899) — John Clark Ridpath’s illustrated one-volume popular history of the United States from aboriginal times through colonization, Revolution, early republic, Civil War, Reconstruction, and late-nineteenth-century administrations through Cleveland’s second term. Read source page
olcott-life-of-william-mckinley-volume-2 — [source] The Life of William McKinley, Volume II (Olcott, 1916) — Charles S. Olcott’s second volume of his William McKinley biography, covering McKinley’s presidency from intervention in Cuba and the Spanish-American War through the peace settlement, Philippines, Puerto Rico, Cuba, China and the Open Door, the 1900 reelection, second inaugural outlook, assassination at Buffalo, and memorial conclusion. Read source page

Read source page

chernow-house-of-morgan — [source] The House of Morgan: An American Banking Dynasty and the Rise of Modern Finance (Chernow, 1990/2010) — Ron Chernow’s history of the Morgan banking dynasty and Morgan-connected firms, tracing George Peabody, Junius Morgan, J. P. Morgan Sr., J. P. Morgan Jr., Morgan Grenfell, Morgan Guaranty, and Morgan Stanley from nineteenth-century Anglo-American merchant banking through railroad finance, industrial consolidation, panics, World War I finance, New Deal reform, Glass-Steagall, and late-twentieth-century market finance. wall-andrew-carnegie — [source] Andrew Carnegie (Wall, 1989/1970) — Joseph Frazier Wall’s major biography of Andrew Carnegie, covering Dunfermline origins, immigration, Pennsylvania Railroad apprenticeship, Civil War and wartime profits, diversified investments, iron and steel, Frick and Homestead, empire-building, anti-imperial politics, the Gospel of Wealth, philanthropy, peace activism, Skibo, World War I, and Carnegie’s death. sources/allen-only-yesterday.title: [source] Only Yesterday: An Informal History of the 1920s (Allen, 1931)
sources/allen-only-yesterday.content:
Only Yesterday: An Informal History of the 1920s
Author: Frederick Lewis Allen
Published: Harper & Brothers, 1931 (copyright Frederick Lewis Allen 1931; Agnes Rogers Allen 1959)
Working text: Open Road Integrated Media ebook edition, 2015 (ISBN 978-1-5040-1137-2; AA hash fbdb17eb865de244038dd09b1e3b3f4e)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/allen-only-yesterday.txt
Extract stats: 4,234 lines · ~118,806 words · 720,430 bytes (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1920-45 into the United States 1866–1919 wiki for the Armistice–1919 bridge. Its strongest overlap with this folder is the era definition from 11 November 1918, Chapter I (May 1919 prelude), and the early postwar chapters on demobilization, League fight, and Red Scare onset. The main 1920s body (Coolidge prosperity, ballyhoo, Bull Market, Crash) remains primarily for the 1920–45 wiki. Pair with Paxson Chapters XXV–XXVII used selectively for immediate postwar spillover.
Completeness Assessment
The clean digital EPUB extract is complete for wiki use. After modern Open Road marketing front matter and a machine table of contents, the body runs Preface → Chapters I–XIV → Appendix (“Sources and Obligations”) → Index. Modern Open Road author-promo trailer follows the copyright block at the tail and is not part of Allen’s 1931 text. Chapter structure matches the imprint contents list.
Overview
Allen frames the eleven years from the Armistice of 11 November 1918 to the stock-market panic culminating on 13 November 1929 as a distinct era—“the Post-war Decade”—whose destruction of Coolidge (and Hoover) Prosperity the crash hastened and dramatized. Writing in 1931 while recollection was still fresh, he deliberately emphasizes the changing state of the public mind, fads, fashions, and follies that touched daily life, and leaves much foreign policy to later historians. He acknowledges debt to Mark Sullivan’s method in Our Own Times and lists principal sources in an appendix rather than footnotes.
For this wiki the book is the natural 1920s narrative spine: demobilization and the League fight, the Big Red Scare, convalescence into mass amusements, the revolution in manners and morals, Harding and the oil scandals, Coolidge Prosperity and business culture, ballyhoo and Lindbergh, highbrow revolt, Prohibition and Capone, the Florida boom, the Big Bull Market, Crash, and the bitter 1930–31 aftermath. It pairs with Allen’s sequel Since Yesterday (1930s) once that source page is built, and later with Groves, Conant, Elliott Roosevelt, and the Nevins & Hill Ford volumes for wartime and industrial threads.
Narrative Source Flow
Preface
Lines 69–82. ~560 words.
This book is an attempt to tell, and in some measure to interpret, the story of what in the future may be considered a distinct era in American history: the eleven years between the end of the war with Germany (November 11, 1918) and the stock-market panic which culminated on November 13, 1929, hastening and dramatizing the destruction of what had been known as Coolidge (and Hoover) Prosperity. Writing so soon after the event means breaking new ground; many events of those years, Allen notes, have never been chronicled in full—including a continuous narrative of the Harding scandals and of the Big Bull Market as economic and social phenomenon. A contemporary history is bound to be anything but definitive, yet half the enjoyment of writing it has lain in reducing to order a mass of material untouched by previous historians. Emphasis on the public mind and on sometimes trivial preoccupations is deliberate: the close-range writer has a special chance to record fads, fashions, and follies while recollection is fresh, and may leave foreign affairs whose full effect is not yet measurable to subsequent historians. Allen credits Mark Sullivan’s Our Own Times for developing this method, and adds an appendix of principal sources in place of footnotes.
Chapter I — Prelude: May, 1919
Lines 83–146. ~4,560 words.
If time were suddenly to turn back to the earliest days of the Post-war Decade, what would seem strange? Allen follows a moderately well-to-do young couple—Mr. and Mrs. Smith of any large city—through an ordinary day in May 1919, six months after the Armistice, when war ways have largely given way to peace but the decade’s profound alterations have hardly begun. Men’s fashions move glacially; Mrs. Smith’s skirt hangs six inches from the ground, stockings are black or tan not flesh-colored, powder is possible but paint still frowned on by the well-brought-up, hair is long, and short hair still smells of radicalism. Vitamins are unknown; tabloids are not yet born (the New York Daily News will appear 26 June 1919). Front-page news is the Navy seaplane NC-4’s Azores route, the Peace Conference, Victory Loan, returning transports, strikes, Mayor Ole Hanson against the I.W.W., woman suffrage, and Henry Ford’s libel suit. Babe Ruth is still obscure on the Red Sox; Dempsey–Willard is set for Toledo; golf has not yet become the business man’s weekly ritual.
High Cost of Living dominates breakfast talk—milk, steak, butter, eggs, and rents far above 1914. Mr. Smith’s open car (only about a tenth of 1919 production closed) may be a Ford Model T cranked by hand; registered passenger cars are under seven million versus over twenty-three million a decade later; speed limits average about twenty miles an hour. At the office, business is looking up after post-Armistice uncertainty; labor demands and Bolshevism and stock speculation are the clouds. Radio broadcasting does not yet exist for the Smiths. Allen closes the prelude by listing the decade’s coming furniture of mind—Coué, Dayton, cross-word puzzles, Teapot Dome, Coral Gables, Sacco and Vanzetti, speakeasies, Capone, Lindbergh—and leaves the Post-war Decade lying before them.
Chapter II — Back to Normalcy
Lines 147–276. ~9,660 words.
Early on the morning of 11 November 1918, Woodrow Wilson writes in pencil on White House stationery that the armistice is signed, everything America fought for is accomplished, and it will now be the country’s duty to assist by example, sober counsel, and material aid in establishing just democracy throughout the world. Allen reads the message as Puritan schoolmaster, moral idealist, and dogmatic prophet of democracy—Wilsonian and almost Lincolnian—yet notes that Lincoln did not live to see what happens to idealism in a post-war decade. The 11th of November is carnival in the streets; then come demobilization, cancellation of war contracts, the slow return of the A.E.F., and the bitter fight over the Treaty and the League.
Lodge, the Italian vote and Fiume, the secret memorandum entrusted to Henry White for Balfour, Clemenceau, and Nitti, Borah and the irreconcilables, and Wilson’s western tour and collapse fill the political center. Harding emerges as the available man of “normalcy”; Cox and Roosevelt lose in 1920. Allen ends with Wilson in S Street on Armistice Day five years after the war—supported so he will not fall—declaring that fools who resist Providence will meet utter destruction, and dying three months later.
Chapter III — The Big Red Scare
Lines 277–436. ~9,630 words.
If Americans turned a deaf ear to Wilson’s League in the early Post-war Decade, it was not only weariness of foreign entanglements. They were listening to rumors of radical conspiracy, cocked for bombs and Bolshevist armies, millions of otherwise reasonable citizens thinking Red revolution might begin next month or next week. Front pages shout strikes and anti-Bolshevist riots; radicals shoot Armistice Day paraders in Centralia and a white I.W.W. member is lynched from a bridge; Socialist assemblymen are expelled in New York; an Indiana jury acquits a man for killing an alien who shouted “To hell with the United States.”
Palmer’s raids, the Fighting Quaker, deportations, super-patriotic societies, blacklists that touch even charities and theatres and colleges (Frankfurter, Chafee, Dewey, Main Street), race riot in Chicago, and the Wall Street explosion of 16 September 1920 carry the narrative. By the time the explosion’s mystery is still unsolved years later, Allen judges that the country was already coming to its senses enough to see that no such plot could command more than a handful of fanatics—had it come a few months earlier, the indirect consequences might have been uglier still.
Chapter IV — America Convalescent
Lines 437–498. ~3,390 words.
The Big Red Scare dies slowly: insufficient cause for the panic; Communism localized in Europe; radicalism ebbing at home; Palmer’s methods scaring many Reds into “pale pinkness”; A. F. of L. leaders leaning over backward toward conservatism; wets acquiring a belated concern for personal liberty. More important, the temper of war’s aftermath gives way to the temper of peace—like an overworked business man beginning vacation, the country learns again to relax and amuse itself.
Mah-jongg, radio, confession magazines, Main Street, The Sheik, If Winter Comes, and above all the Hall–Mills murder of 16 September 1922 near New Brunswick feed a national appetite for diversion and sensation. Sacco and Vanzetti run as a recurring political and emotional storm; when the headlines finally scream execution, men shiver, wonder whether justice or hideous mistake, and turn to where Lindbergh is flying and what General Motors is doing.
Chapter V — The Revolution in Manners and Morals
Lines 499–634. ~11,210 words.
A first-class revolt against the accepted American order is under way in the early Post-war Decade, but Lenin has nothing to do with it. Shock troops are sons and daughters of well-to-do families; defiance is spoken across the breakfast table. While elders still shiver at the Red Menace they awake to the Problem of the Younger Generation. The old code—woman as guardian of morality, innocent waiting for the altar, a double standard for men—cracks under war, prosperity, the automobile, prohibition’s hypocrisies, Freudian talk, and freer manners.
Skirts rise, bobbed hair moves from radical stigma (1918) to boom business contested by hairdressers and barbers, cosmetics and cigarettes spread, petting and companionate-marriage talk alarm the pulpits, and divorce statistics and sex in fiction and film mark the change. Middletown evidence and fashion economics run through the chapter. Not until the decade nears its end do signs appear that the revolutionists are learning to be at home in the freer code, less obsessed with sex, and to discover among the ruins of the old dispensation a new set of enduring satisfactions.
Chapter VI — Harding and the Scandals
Lines 635–856. ~11,260 words.
Allen opens with Harry M. Daugherty’s 1926 refusal to testify before a federal grand jury—personal attorney to the Hardings, Attorney-General, relations “of the most confidential character,” answers that might tend to incriminate. On 4 March 1921 Wilson limps from the White House; Harding is sworn in; the reign of normalcy begins. The Ohio Gang, Daugherty, Jess Smith, Forbes and the Veterans’ Bureau, Fall, Doheny, Sinclair, Teapot Dome and Elk Hills, the Continental Trading Company Liberty-bond packages to Blackmer, O’Neil, Stewart, and Sinclair, Senate investigation, and the slow unraveling after Harding’s death in 1923 fill the narrative.
Coolidge inherits the mess; prosecutions and political embarrassment drag through the decade. When Hoover and Coolidge finally take part in dedicating Harding’s tomb in June 1931, Allen notes a certain restraint—it is not so easy as in 1923 to compose panegyrics on the good-natured man who had “taught us the power of brotherliness.”
Chapter VII — Coolidge Prosperity
Lines 857–987. ~8,520 words.
Business is booming when Harding dies; by kerosene lamp in a Vermont farmhouse Colonel John Coolidge administers the presidential oath to Calvin. The depression of 1921 has given way to improvement in 1922 and rushing revival in 1923. Stock prices on 2 August 1923 still suggest no unreasonable optimism—Steel 87, small volume—and the Big Bull Market is still far ahead, but the tide of prosperity is in full flood. Allen traces the jagged statistical path of the decade to the Everest of 1929 and the abyss of 1930–31.
Mass production, installment buying, the automobile and good roads, electrification, chain stores, advertising’s rise from business to self-styled profession to, among practitioners, a “racket,” service clubs, Rotary and boosters, the fusion of religion and business (The Man Nobody Knows), and Coolidge’s discreet obeisance before the great god business structure the chapter. Statesmanship of a sort Coolidge represents: encourage prosperity without hot water; accept the inevitable; do not try to be bolder than circumstances safely permit.
Chapter VIII — The Ballyhoo Years
Lines 988–1219. ~12,380 words.
One striking mark of Coolidge Prosperity is the unparalleled rapidity and unanimity with which millions fix attention on tremendous trifles—a heavyweight fight, a murder trial, a new car model, a transatlantic flight. Most causes célèbres are unimportant by traditional historical measure; that they could engage unprecedented numbers is not. Allen reviews Hall–Mills and the “pig woman,” Floyd Collins in the Kentucky cave, sports idols, beauty contests, cross-word puzzles, radio crazes, and above all Charles A. Lindbergh’s flight as the heroism of a stunt flyer who crossed the ocean for a money prize.
The Dayton Scopes trial is told at length: Bryan on the stand before reason as prosecutor, Raulston’s mercy, Scopes guilty and fined one hundred dollars, the law upheld on technicality but Fundamentalism losing in civilized opinion as the slow drift from certainty continues. By early 1928 ballyhoo’s bloom may be departing—Lindbergh has spoiled the public for lesser heroes; Sacco–Vanzetti and the 1928 campaign remind a well-fed people of public issues; and a ten-point gain in Radio common in a single day promises more immediate benefits than all the non-stop flyers and heavyweight champions in the world.
Chapter IX — The Revolt of the Highbrows
Lines 1220–1309. ~5,830 words.
Allen opens with Fitzgerald’s generation that found all Gods dead, all wars fought, all faiths in man shaken. Wartime social compulsion becomes peacetime habit—drives, quotas, canned publicity, the man who grips his pocketbook feeling mass opinion. Intellectuals revolt: against puritanism and censorship, against the exaltation of the business man, against the reformer (by 1925 a term of contempt among them), often in religious skepticism, united in scorn of the bourgeois majority held responsible for prohibition, Fundamentalism, and other repressions—Babbitts, Rotarians, the Klan, Service-with-a-Smile, boosters and super-salesmen, with Mencken as tone-setter.
Disillusionment and the lost generation’s meager pleasure in self-pity cannot find peace; Allen closes on groping for new values among those for whom the new day heralded in wartime had turned to night before it arrived.
Chapter X — Alcohol and Al Capone
Lines 1310–1431. ~7,770 words.
Had one told the average American in 1919 that prohibition would be the most violently explosive public issue of the nineteen-twenties, he would have thought the prophecy mad. Rum-ships outside the twelve-mile limit, hijacked beer trucks, stills by the carload, fashionable contraband cocktails, speakeasy grills, and Capone in an armor-plated car would have dropped his jaw. The Eighteenth Amendment, ratified to take effect 16 January 1920, had seemed to settle the issue.
Allen traces the ease of final dry victory after generations of uphill fighting, then the collapse of enforcement, wet and dry geography, corruption, Chicago gang war, Capone’s rise, rackets beyond liquor, and the Wickersham Commission’s paradoxical 1931 report—sorry inability to dry the country, individual commissioners split, corporate vote for further trial—satirized in Flaccus’s summary in F.P.A.’s column. As the decade bows out, prohibition, gangster, and racket problems remain unsolved for the nineteen-thirties; still the rum-running launch slips across the river and tabloid-readers find adventure in gangster killings.
Chapter XI — Home, Sweet Florida
Lines 1432–1547. ~5,960 words.
Allen quotes a bank vice-president’s unbuttoned 1925 rhetoric in the Miamian—palms, sun-kissed sky, Caribbean breeze—as the Florida boom hits its height amid Scopes aftermath, Red Grange, and The Man Nobody Knows. Miami becomes one frenzied real-estate exchange: thousands of offices and agents, binder boys, Coral Gables and the American tropics as sales religion, lot prices in a fever unmatched in ninety years.
The mayors’ “Fiesta of the American Tropics” at the turn of 1925–26 promises Love, Good Fellowship, and Sublime Beauty; by New Year’s the suspicion insinuates itself that new buyers are not appearing as they should. Collapse, bank strain, and the shift of speculative infection from Flagler Street to Broad and Wall follow. Florida house-lots a bad bet? Then, asks a public still enthralled by Coolidge Prosperity, what else is there to bet on? The Big Bull Market is getting under way.
Chapter XII — The Big Bull Market
Lines 1548–1738. ~9,540 words.
One day in February 1928 an investor asks an astute banker about common stocks; the banker thinks them dangerously high and would wait. By conservative canons he is right: Coolidge Prosperity confidence has already lifted prices far since 1924. Through 1927 speculation increases; brokers’ loans rise from about 2.82 billion to 3.56 billion; a record week of trading hits in December. After-dinner talk from New York to the lowliest village runs to the market.
Allen follows the 1928–29 advance: Radio and the new-era argument, investment trusts, rejection of “ten times earnings,” breaks in June and December 1928 that teach the lesson “when there is a break it is a good time to buy,” call money at 8 and 9 percent explained away, and the vision of an America set free from poverty and toil—cars, airplanes, high-tension wires, skyscrapers, and smartly dressed men and women spending with money won by being far-sighted enough, way back in 1929, to foresee what was going to happen.
Chapter XIII — Crash!
Lines 1739–1855. ~6,050 words.
Early in September the stock market breaks, recovers to a Times averages high on 19 September even above 3 September, then slips farther; by 4 October Steel, Can, General Electric, and Radio look like bargains to those trained by earlier breaks. Brokers’ loans still mount to a new high about $6.8 billion on 2 October—margin buyers undiminished. Then comes the cascade of mid-October and the panic days: 23 October’s Niagara of liquidation; Thursday the 24th’s forced selling as margins exhaust, the ticker lagging, the roar of panic on the floor; the midday bankers’ pool at Morgan’s—Mitchell, Wiggin, Potter, Prosser, Lamont, Baker—forty millions apiece to keep trading orderly, not to peg prices.
Black Tuesday and the weeks that follow shatter the price structure. Allen’s close: the Big Bull Market had been more than the climax of a business cycle; it had been the climax of a cycle in American mass thinking and mass emotion. With it gone and prosperity going, Americans face an altered world. The psychological climate is changing. The Post-war Decade has come to its close. An era has ended.
Chapter XIV — Aftermath: 1930–31
Lines 1856–1949. ~5,780 words.
Not without long and unhappy protest does the country accept the breakdown of Coolidge–Hoover Prosperity—bitter for a Republican party that had half forgotten the business cycle’s independence of political policies, bitterest for Hoover who had spoken of abolishing poverty. After the market goes over Niagara, the country turns to the President. He promises tax reduction, conferences against wage cuts, public works, and a campaign of reassurance that “conditions” are “fundamentally sound.” Mellon, Lamont, Barnes, and Hoover set dates for recovery; a Little Bull Market in early 1930 regains much ground, then sickens in April as the Coué formula fails against organic disease.
Allen lists diseases: overproduction of capital and goods; artificial commodity prices and pools; silver’s collapse; gold shifts to France and the United States; foreign unrest; the self-generating effect of depression; and the profound psychological reaction from 1929’s exuberance. Wheat crashes despite the Farm Board; industrial production sinks; banks fail including the Bank of the United States in New York; unemployment approaches some six million; apple salesmen stand on corners. Fashion and manners show armistice in the moral revolution—freedom kept, excited sense of smashing taboos gone. Allen ends: the stream of time often doubles on its course, but always makes for itself a new channel.
Appendix — Sources and Obligations
Lines 1950–1991. ~1,410 words.
Allen records principal debts: the Lynds’ Middletown; the Beards’ Rise of American Civilization (including the Washington Conference); William Allen White on Wilson, Harding, and Coolidge; Charles Merz on prohibition and related books; World Almanac, New York Times Index, and Times files. Chapter notes point to Baker on Wilson and the Peace Conference, Chafee on free speech and the Palmer raids, Nystrom on fashion, Lippmann and Krutch on morals and disillusion, Ravage and Bliven on oil and the Ohio Gang, Stuart Chase on prosperity, Silas Bent on ballyhoo, Pasley on Capone, Vanderblue on Florida, Whitney on the Exchange in the panic, and James Truslow Adams on “Presidential Prosperity.” Personal thanks close with Dorothy Penrose Allen. Dated Scarsdale, New York, June 1931.
Index
Lines 1992–4234. ~5,000 words of index entries.
Extensive subject and name index (A & P Gypsies through the alphabet) useful for locating persons, episodes, and themes across the narrative.
Coverage Guide
Mine first as the period’s popular-contemporary spine for 1919–1931. Chapters I–IV support demobilization, League and normalcy politics, Red Scare, and early-1920s cultural convalescence. Chapters V–X are strongest for manners, Harding scandals, Coolidge business culture, ballyhoo, intellectuals, and Prohibition/crime. Chapters XI–XIV are the core speculative cycle: Florida, Bull Market, Crash, and Hoover-era aftermath into 1931. Use the Appendix as a contemporary bibliography map, not as later historiography.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 69–82: Allen’s era definition (11 Nov 1918–13 Nov 1929) and method (public mind, fads, close range).
Lines 83–146: May 1919 baseline day (prices, cars, news, what the Smiths have never heard of).
Lines 277–436: Red Scare arc from Centralia and Palmer to Wall Street explosion.
Lines 499–634: revolution in manners and morals; bobbed hair, youth code, armistice at decade’s end.
Lines 635–856: Daugherty epigraph; Teapot Dome / Continental Trading Company bond chain.
Lines 988–1219: ballyhoo structure; Dayton trial; Lindbergh as age’s hero.
Lines 1432–1738: Florida boom to Bull Market new-era vision.
Lines 1739–1855: September–October 1929 breaks; 24 October; bankers’ pool; era’s end.
Lines 1856–1949: Hoover reassurance campaign; seven “diseases”; 1930–31 social mood.
Lines 1950–1991: Allen’s own source map for cross-checks.

Suggested Future Pages

Coolidge Prosperity — concept page on business prestige, installment buying, advertising, and political quietism.
Big Bull Market and Crash of 1929 — event cluster from 1928 advance through October–November 1929.
Prohibition and the Bootleg Economy — concept page linking Volstead enforcement, speakeasies, Capone, and Wickersham.
Revolution in Manners and Morals — concept page on youth, sex codes, fashion, and the late-decade armistice.
Big Red Scare (1919–20) — event page on Palmer, Centralia, deportations, and the scare’s fade.
Florida Real Estate Boom — event page as prelude to Wall Street speculation.
Ballyhoo and Mass Hero-Worship — concept page on Hall–Mills, Dayton, sports, and Lindbergh.

Related Sources

Since Yesterday — Allen’s companion informal history of the 1930s (to be added).
Nevins & Hill Ford volumes (expansion; decline and rebirth) — industrial continuity across the same decades (to be added).
Library peers in United States 1866–1919 wiki (e.g. Paxson’s postwar chapters) — bridge from Wilson’s war into Allen’s decade.

Notes on Scope
Near-contemporary informal history (composed by June 1931), not archival monograph. Exceptionally strong on atmosphere, sequence of public crazes, and the speculative psychology of 1925–29; individual scandal and market details should be cross-checked against specialized sources when building detailed entity or event pages. Foreign affairs are intentionally thin by Allen’s own design.

sources/blaine-twenty-years-of-congress-.title: [source] Twenty Years of Congress, Volume I (Blaine, 1884)
sources/blaine-twenty-years-of-congress-.content:
Twenty Years of Congress, Volume I
Author: James G. Blaine
Published: Henry Bill Publishing Company, 1884
Working text: Hathi-style OCR ZIP via Anna’s Archive (oclc 772582529, hash e17011b7cba09af555248db9c8340d17)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/blaine-twenty-years-of-congress-volume-1.txt
Extract stats: 686 OCR page files · 36,058 lines · ~283,176 words · 1,716,256 bytes
Completeness Assessment
The OCR ZIP appears complete as Volume I of Blaine’s two-volume work. It includes title/copyright pages, a long contents section, Chapters I–XXVI, appendix material, and the end matter for the volume. It is not the whole work: Volume II continues the congressional and Reconstruction narrative.
Overview
James G. Blaine wrote as a major Republican politician and participant-observer rather than as a detached later historian. Volume I is therefore valuable both as narrative history and as a Republican political memory of the Civil War generation. For the United States 1866–1919 wiki, its main importance is the background to Reconstruction and postwar congressional politics: the party revolution of 1860, secession, wartime legislation, emancipation, finance, Lincoln, Congress, and the political inheritance that shaped the years after 1865.
This volume should be paired with Twenty Years of Congress, Volume II for the Reconstruction continuation, Recent History of the United States for later synthesis, and The Life of William McKinley, Volume II for Republican politics after the congressional generation Blaine describes.
Narrative Source Flow
Front Matter and Contents
Lines 31–1063. The title and contents present the work’s scope: from Lincoln to Garfield, with a review of the events that produced the political revolution of 1860. The contents are unusually detailed, making them a useful map of Blaine’s political priorities.
Chapters I–VIII — Sectional Crisis and the Political Revolution of 1860
Lines 1064–9056. The opening chapters review the party and sectional conflicts that led to Republican victory and secession. Blaine covers slavery politics, the decline of older party alignments, the Kansas-Nebraska struggle, the Dred Scott atmosphere, Democratic division, Republican organization, Lincoln, and the rupture that made congressional government central to the crisis.
Chapters IX–XIII — Secession, Lincoln, War Powers, and the Early War
Lines 9057–14132. These chapters move through secession, Lincoln’s accession, the opening of war, the special session of Congress, military and civil authority, loyalty, border-state problems, and the emergency powers required to preserve the Union.
Chapters XIV–XVIII — Congress, Finance, Emancipation, and Wartime Policy
Lines 14133–19415. Blaine gives sustained attention to wartime congressional action: revenue, loans, legal-tender notes, banking, military organization, confiscation, slavery, emancipation, enlistment, and the expanding administrative state of war.
Chapters XIX–XXIII — Politics of War and the Presidential Struggle
Lines 19416–24098. The middle-late chapters follow wartime political conflict, public opinion, Democratic opposition, constitutional argument, Chase, Lincoln, Congress, and the presidential struggle that made the election of 1864 a referendum on Union policy.
Chapters XXIV–XXVI — End of War and Transition to Reconstruction
Lines 24099–28269. The final chapters carry the story toward war’s end and the political terms on which peace and Reconstruction would begin. They are useful for understanding the congressional premises that Volume II then develops in the postwar setting.
Appendix
Lines 28270 onward. The appendix preserves supporting political and documentary material useful for checking Blaine’s narrative against congressional and party records.
Coverage Guide
This volume is most useful for pages on the origins of Reconstruction, the Republican Party, wartime Congress, Union finance, emancipation policy, Lincoln’s leadership, and the congressional meaning of Union victory. It is less directly about 1866–1919 events than about the constitutional and partisan inheritance that shaped them.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 1064–9056: party realignment before 1860 and the political revolution that made the Republican Party dominant.
Lines 9057–14132: secession, Lincoln, emergency government, and early-war congressional authority.
Lines 14133–19415: wartime finance, banking, legal tender, confiscation, emancipation, and administrative growth.
Lines 19416–24098: wartime opposition, public opinion, Chase, Lincoln, and the election of 1864.
Lines 24099–28269: transition from war to Reconstruction and the premises carried into Volume II.

Suggested Future Pages

Congressional Reconstruction — concept page using both Blaine volumes.
Republican Party after the Civil War — concept/entity page on party identity, Union victory, and congressional power.
Legal Tender and Civil War Finance — concept page connecting wartime finance to later greenback and gold-standard politics.
Election of 1864 — event page as a wartime referendum.

Related Sources

Twenty Years of Congress, Volume II — continuation into Reconstruction and later congressional politics.
Recent History of the United States — later synthetic treatment of Reconstruction and the Gilded Age.
The Life of William McKinley, Volume II — Republican political inheritance in the later McKinley era.
United States: A History — popular one-volume narrative covering the same war and postwar transition.

Notes on Scope
Blaine was a political actor and Republican leader. His narrative is indispensable as a participant’s Republican account, but source pages that synthesize Reconstruction should balance it with later histories and primary records where possible.

sources/blaine-twenty-years-of-congress-.title: [source] Twenty Years of Congress, Volume II (Blaine, 1886)
sources/blaine-twenty-years-of-congress-.content:
Twenty Years of Congress, Volume II
Author: James G. Blaine
Published: Henry Bill Publishing Company, 1886
Working text: Hathi-style OCR ZIP via Anna’s Archive (oclc 772582529, hash e1da17bebe06cef0d2ee8e9b6a6450d1)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/blaine-twenty-years-of-congress-volume-2.txt
Extract stats: 766 OCR page files · 36,782 lines · ~333,011 words · 2,008,154 bytes
Completeness Assessment
The OCR ZIP appears complete as Volume II of Blaine’s two-volume work. It includes title/copyright pages, contents for Volume II, Chapters I–XXIX, appendices embedded in the volume, and the concluding matter. Together with Volume I, it forms Blaine’s full two-volume congressional history.
Overview
Volume II is the more directly relevant Blaine volume for this wiki because it centers on Reconstruction and the congressional settlement after the Civil War. It follows Andrew Johnson, congressional Republicans, constitutional amendments, impeachment, the reorganization of Southern governments, civil rights, party conflict, Grant, finance, and the political movement from Lincoln’s death toward Garfield.
Its value is twofold: it provides detailed congressional-political narrative for the 1865–1881 core of the wiki, and it preserves how a leading Republican statesman explained Reconstruction only a short time after the events. It pairs naturally with Paxson for a later synthesis and with Ridpath for popular late-nineteenth-century memory.
Narrative Source Flow
Front Matter and Contents
Lines 29–1240. The contents identify Volume II as the Reconstruction and postwar continuation of the work. The chapters trace Johnson, Congress, constitutional amendments, impeachment, Southern readmission, civil-rights and suffrage politics, and the later Republican era.
Chapters I–IV — Lincoln’s Death, Johnson, and the Opening of Reconstruction
Lines 1241–4987. Blaine begins with the transition from Lincoln to Johnson and the uncertain legal and political meaning of restoration. The central issue is who would control Reconstruction: the President, Congress, or the defeated states themselves.
Chapters V–VIII — Congressional Reconstruction and Constitutional Settlement
Lines 4988–9713. These chapters follow the hardening conflict between Johnson and Congress, the conditions for readmission, the Fourteenth Amendment, Southern loyalism, freedpeople, federal authority, and the attempt to define citizenship and representation after slavery.
Chapters IX–XI — Impeachment, Tenure of Office, and Political Crisis
Lines 9714–13994. Blaine treats the constitutional struggle around Johnson’s conduct, the Tenure of Office Act, impeachment, Senate trial, and acquittal. These chapters are central for any page on the presidency-versus-Congress conflict after the Civil War.
Chapters XII–XV — Grant, Southern Reconstruction, and National Policy
Lines 13995–19679. The narrative moves into Grant-era politics, Southern state governments, enforcement problems, public debt, currency, taxation, foreign and territorial issues, and Republican management of postwar national consolidation.
Chapters XVI–XX — Civil Rights, Amendments, Finance, and Sectional Politics
Lines 19680–24051. Blaine connects constitutional and civil-rights issues to the practical politics of Congress. These chapters should be mined for the Fifteenth Amendment, enforcement, amnesty, public credit, party disputes, and the continuing conflict over the meaning of Union victory.
Chapters XXI–XXIX — Later Grant Era to Garfield
Lines 24052 onward. The closing chapters carry the political story toward the 1870s and Garfield, including party alignments, elections, congressional leadership, sectional reconciliation, and the settlement or exhaustion of Reconstruction-era issues.
Coverage Guide
This volume should be the first Blaine source mined for Reconstruction. It is strong on Johnson, congressional authority, constitutional amendments, impeachment, readmission, civil rights, enforcement, Grant-era Republican politics, and the transition from war politics to Gilded Age party conflict.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 1241–4987: Lincoln-to-Johnson transition and opening dispute over Reconstruction authority.
Lines 4988–9713: Fourteenth Amendment, congressional conditions, and state readmission.
Lines 9714–13994: Johnson impeachment and the Tenure of Office conflict.
Lines 13995–19679: Grant-era Southern policy, finance, enforcement, and national consolidation.
Lines 19680–24051: civil rights, suffrage, amendments, public credit, and sectional politics.
Lines 24052 onward: movement from Reconstruction politics toward the Garfield era.

Suggested Future Pages

Reconstruction Acts — event/concept page on congressional terms for Southern readmission.
Fourteenth Amendment — concept/event page on citizenship, representation, and congressional power.
Impeachment of Andrew Johnson — event page on Tenure of Office, House charges, Senate trial, and acquittal.
Fifteenth Amendment — concept/event page on suffrage and enforcement.
Grant Administration and Reconstruction — concept/entity page on enforcement, civil rights, and Republican policy.

Related Sources

Twenty Years of Congress, Volume I — prewar and wartime congressional background.
Recent History of the United States — later synthesis of Reconstruction and postwar politics.
United States: A History — popular one-volume late-nineteenth-century narrative of the same postwar era.
The Life of William McKinley, Volume II — later Republican presidency and party memory after Blaine’s generation.

Notes on Scope
As with Volume I, Blaine writes from within Republican political memory. That makes the work especially valuable as evidence for how congressional Republicans understood Reconstruction, but detailed synthesis pages should keep the partisan vantage visible.

sources/chernow-house-of-morgan.title: [source] The House of Morgan: An American Banking Dynasty and the Rise of Modern Finance (Chernow, 1990/2010)
sources/chernow-house-of-morgan.content:
The House of Morgan
Author: Ron Chernow
Published: Grove Press / Open Road Integrated Media ebook, 2010; originally 1990
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (isbn13 9780802144652, hash 6ce111269eae8cd9e681efbf56fd5518)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/chernow-house-of-morgan.txt (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Extract stats: 14,949 lines · ~334,477 words · 2,102,684 bytes
Overview
Chernow’s The House of Morgan is a history of the Morgan banking dynasty and its institutional descendants: the London and New York Morgan partnerships, J. P. Morgan & Co., Morgan Grenfell, Morgan Guaranty, and Morgan Stanley. The book’s prologue presents the old House of Morgan as both private bank and quasi-public financial power: a firm that sold American securities in London, financed railroads and industrial combinations, rescued governments and markets, and generated a century of suspicion about banker influence.
For this United States 1866–1919 wiki, Part One: The Baronial Age, 1838–1913 and the opening of Part Two: The Diplomatic Age, 1913–1948 are the core material. They cover George Peabody, Junius Morgan, J. P. Morgan Sr., railroad finance, the gold-standard rescue of 1895, the creation of U.S. Steel, the Panic of 1907, the Pujo investigation, Morgan’s death in 1913, the Federal Reserve transition, and World War I finance under J. P. Morgan Jr. Later sections extend far beyond the wiki’s chronological scope but are valuable for tracing the afterlife of Morgan institutions and the transformation from relationship banking to securities markets and casino finance.
The EPUB structure is: front matter; contents; prologue; Part One, “The Baronial Age, 1838–1913,” Chapters 1–8; Part Two, “The Diplomatic Age, 1913–1948,” Chapters 9–24; Part Three, “The Casino Age, 1948–1989,” Chapters 25–36; acknowledgments; notes; bibliography; index.
Narrative Source Flow
Prologue
Lines 290–338. Framing of the House of Morgan as American banking empire, transatlantic web, private bank, quasi-central bank, financial ambassador, and source of conspiracy theories about banker power.
Part One — The Baronial Age, 1838–1913
Lines 339–1444. The nineteenth-century and Progressive Era Morgan world: Peabody, Junius Morgan, Pierpont Morgan, railroads, industrial consolidation, gold rescue, U.S. Steel, Panic of 1907, Pujo, Titanic, and Pierpont’s death.
Chapter 1 — Scrooge
Lines 343–438. George Peabody in London, American state debt defaults, British capital, reputation, Maryland finance, early merchant banking, and Peabody’s austere personal style.
Chapter 2 — Polonius
Lines 439–526. Junius Spencer Morgan, Hartford family background, Morgan discipline, London standing, paternal control, and the family/business precepts inherited by Pierpont.
Chapter 3 — Prince
Lines 527–630. Young Pierpont Morgan as Wall Street agent of British capital, post-Civil War railroad boom, European investors, corrupt finance, Gould/Drew/Tweed context, and Morgan’s self-image as defender of sound capital.
Chapter 4 — Corsair
Lines 631–798. Morgan’s domestic and social world, 23 Wall Street, Edison Electric financing, Gilded Age display, art collecting, railroads, and the contrast between Morgan reserve and nouveau riche spectacle.
Chapter 5 — Corner
Lines 799–966. Gold standard crisis of 1895, Treasury weakness, Argentina/London chain reaction, Cleveland administration, Morgan syndicate, and private rescue of federal gold reserves.
Chapter 6 — Trust
Lines 967–1144. Morgan industrial combinations, railroad reorganizations, General Electric, U.S. Steel, the banker’s role in stabilizing or concentrating corporate capitalism, and criticism of “money trust” power.
Chapter 7 — Panic
Lines 1145–1260. Panic of 1907, Knickerbocker Trust, Morgan as private crisis manager, Wall Street rescue operations, and the episode’s role in exposing the need for central banking reform.
Chapter 8 — Titanic
Lines 1261–1444. Late Pierpont Morgan, Pujo investigation, public attack on the money trust, Titanic-era symbolism, Morgan’s declining health, death in 1913, and the end of baronial banking.
Part Two — The Diplomatic Age, 1913–1948
Lines 1445–4004. Jack Morgan, World War I finance, Anglo-American diplomacy, interwar loans, 1929 crash, New Deal securities reform, Glass-Steagall separation, Morgan Stanley, World War II, and postwar transitions.
Chapter 9 — Metamorphosis
Lines 1449–1590. J. P. Morgan Jr. after 1913, Federal Reserve context, transition from Pierpont’s personal command to a more institutional and diplomatic banking age.
Chapter 10 — War
Lines 1591–2034. World War I, Morgan ties to Britain and France, Allied purchasing and loans, neutrality controversy, export finance, and the bank’s role in America’s wartime financial shift.
Chapter 11 — Explosion
Lines 2035–2202. 1920 Wall Street bombing, postwar backlash, Morgan as symbol of finance capitalism, Red Scare setting, and public vulnerability of 23 Wall.
Chapter 12 — Odyssey
Lines 2203–2362. Interwar international lending, reparations/debt diplomacy, Morgan relationships abroad, and the complicated postwar financial order.
Chapter 13 — Jazz
Lines 2363–2478. 1920s financial culture, securities markets, elite banking, and Morgan adaptation to Jazz Age finance.
Chapter 14 — Golden
Lines 2479–2598. Gold, central banks, currency stabilization, and Morgan’s international monetary role in the 1920s.
Chapter 15 — Saint
Lines 2599–2708. Morgan image, probity, social reputation, and the moral code of old-line banking.
Chapter 16 — Crash
Lines 2709–2844. 1929 crash, Morgan actions, market rescue attempts, and limits of private banker authority.
Chapter 17 — Depression
Lines 2845–3028. Depression aftermath, investigations, political hostility to Wall Street, and the collapse of old financial legitimacy.
Chapter 18 — Midget
Lines 3029–3286. New Deal banking reform, Pecora-era scrutiny, Glass-Steagall, and the enforced split between commercial and investment banking.
Chapter 19 — Crack-Up
Lines 3287–3390. Internal division and institutional consequences of reform.
Chapter 20 — Wizard
Lines 3391–3510. Formation and early role of Morgan Stanley in investment banking after Glass-Steagall.
Chapter 21 — Embezzler
Lines 3511–3652. Scandal, reputation risk, and the fragility of Morgan trust culture.
Chapter 22 — Appeasement
Lines 3653–3786. Late-1930s diplomacy, Europe, appeasement context, and banking’s relation to foreign affairs.
Chapter 23 — Hostages
Lines 3787–3914. World War II pressures and Morgan-linked people/institutions caught in geopolitical crisis.
Chapter 24 — Passages
Lines 3915–4004. Transition toward postwar banking order and the end of the older diplomatic age.
Part Three — The Casino Age, 1948–1989
Lines 4005–5870. Postwar-to-1980s transformation: Morgan Guaranty, Morgan Stanley, Morgan Grenfell, Eurodollars, petrodollars, Latin American debt, takeover finance, trading, LBOs, deregulation, and market-driven banking.
Chapters 25–36
Lines 4009–5870. Modern Morgan descendants from relationship banking to securities, trading, global offices, Guinness scandal, Reagan-era boom, crash, and skyscraper-era Morgan Stanley.
Acknowledgments / Notes / Bibliography / Index
Lines 5871–14949. Research acknowledgments, chapter notes, bibliography, and index; notes begin with chapter-by-chapter citations after line 5909.
Coverage Guide
Morgan finance and Gilded Age corporate capitalism
Chapters 3–8 are the strongest material for the 1866–1919 wiki. They show how Morgan capital entered railroads, reorganizations, electrical companies, U.S. Steel, gold-standard rescue, and panic management. This source is especially useful beside Andrew Carnegie, because Morgan’s purchase of Carnegie Steel and formation of U.S. Steel is a hinge between entrepreneurial steel capitalism and banker-led corporate consolidation.
Private banking as quasi-public power
The prologue, Chapter 5, and Chapter 7 are key for a concept page on private finance before the Federal Reserve. Chernow stresses that Morgan’s firm sometimes acted like a central bank: defending the gold standard, organizing syndicates, and coordinating crisis response. This also makes the source important for understanding why Progressive Era critics spoke of a “money trust.”
Anglo-American finance and foreign policy
The prologue, Chapters 1–3, and Chapters 9–12 cover the London-New York axis: Peabody in London, Junius Morgan, Pierpont as Wall Street agent for British capital, and Jack Morgan’s World War I role financing Allied purchasing and loans. For the wiki’s 1914–1919 period, Chapter 10 is the central section.
Industrial combinations and Morgan clients
Chapters 4–6 link Morgan to Edison Electric, General Electric, railroads, U.S. Steel, AT&T, and other industrial giants. Use alongside The Wizard of Menlo Park, A Life of George Westinghouse, and Andrew Carnegie to map the financial layer behind electrical, railroad, and steel systems.
Progressive attack on banker power
Chapters 7–9 provide material for Pujo, panic reform, central banking, and public hostility toward concentrated financial authority. They also pair with Titan for comparison between oil trust/antitrust politics and finance-centered money-trust politics.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 290–338: prologue framing House of Morgan as private bank, financial empire, quasi-central bank, and international political actor.
Lines 343–526: George Peabody and Junius Morgan origins, London capital, American state debt, and inherited Morgan principles.
Lines 527–630: Pierpont Morgan in the post-Civil War railroad boom, European investors, Wall Street corruption, and “sound men” ideology.
Lines 631–798: Edison Electric financing, 23 Wall Street, Gilded Age social setting, and Morgan domestic/collecting world.
Lines 799–966: 1895 gold rescue and private defense of the gold standard.
Lines 967–1144: Morgan industrial combinations, including General Electric and U.S. Steel context.
Lines 1145–1260: Panic of 1907 and Morgan’s private crisis-management role.

sources/chernow-titan-rockefeller.title: [source] Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller, Sr. (Chernow, 1997)
sources/chernow-titan-rockefeller.content:
Titan
Author: Ron Chernow
Published: 1997, Vintage Books / Random House
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 8d25b37bdb67fde72d1effd0b8b39ca1)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/chernow-titan-rockefeller.txt (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Extract stats: 9,921 lines · ~332,977 words · 2,077,798 bytes
Overview
Chernow’s Titan is a long biography of John D. Rockefeller Sr. that treats Rockefeller’s life as a way into the formation of post-Civil War industrial capitalism, the rise of Standard Oil, the public controversy over trusts and monopoly, and the conversion of private fortune into organized philanthropy. The book’s foreword says Rockefeller had often been reduced either to the Standard Oil trust or to a sequence of caricatures; Chernow’s stated aim is to synthesize Rockefeller’s business, religious, domestic, psychological, political, and philanthropic worlds into one portrait.
For this United States 1866–1919 wiki, the source is central for Gilded Age business organization, oil refining, railroad rebates, trust law, antitrust politics, muckraking journalism, Baptist and evangelical moral culture, institutional philanthropy, Rockefeller family succession, and Progressive Era corporate accountability. Later chapters extend beyond 1919 to Rockefeller’s family legacy, estate, grandchildren, death, and memorial reputation; use those later sections mainly for the afterlife of Rockefeller’s fortune and name.
The EPUB structure is: front matter; foreword; Prelude, “Poison Tongue”; Chapters 1–35; notes; acknowledgments; bibliography; author/copyright matter. Notes begin after Chapter 35 and provide source references for letters, archives, newspapers, Ida Tarbell, Henry Demarest Lloyd, Allan Nevins, William O. Inglis interviews, and Rockefeller Archive Center material.
Narrative Source Flow
Foreword
Lines 188–206. Chernow’s research problem: Rockefeller as elusive subject, Standard Oil as over-dominant frame, use of Rockefeller Archive Center material and the 1917–1920 William O. Inglis interviews.
Prelude — Poison Tongue
Lines 208–241. Elderly Rockefeller answering Henry Demarest Lloyd and Ida Tarbell through private authorized-biography interviews, defending Standard Oil and seeking vindication through memory.
Chapter 1 — The Flimflam Man
Lines 242–307. Rockefeller ancestry, German and Puritan lines, father William Avery “Big Bill” Rockefeller, family instability, and the contrast between paternal fraud and maternal discipline.
Chapter 2 — Fires of Revival
Lines 308–447. Moravia and Owego childhood, evangelical revival culture, Eliza Rockefeller’s moral world, schooling, early death and hardship, and the religious habits that shaped Rockefeller’s temperament.
Chapter 3 — Bound to Be Rich
Lines 448–609. Move to Ohio, Cleveland setting, first employment, bookkeeping discipline, Baptist church life, thrift, ambition, and Rockefeller’s entry into business.
Chapter 4 — Baptism in Business
Lines 610–667. Clark and Rockefeller produce commission business, early credit, loans from Big Bill, Civil War-era commercial growth, and habits of accounting and risk control.
Chapter 5 — The Auction
Lines 668–815. Early petroleum industry, Oil Creek, illuminating oil, Drake well, refining opportunity, Cleveland’s transport position, and Rockefeller’s move from produce into oil.
Chapter 6 — The Poetry of the Age
Lines 816–957. Refining expansion, Henry Flagler, wartime/postwar markets, cost control, reinvestment, and the emerging logic of scale and integration.
Chapter 7 — Millionaires’ Row
Lines 958–1019. Cleveland wealth, domestic life, marriage to Laura Spelman, Baptist household culture, Euclid Avenue society, and the contrast between wealth and restraint.
Chapter 8 — Conspirators
Lines 1020–1193. Railroad competition, South Improvement Company, rebates and drawbacks, oil-region revolt, and the first major public conflict over Rockefeller’s methods.
Chapter 9 — The New Monarch
Lines 1194–1297. Standard Oil’s consolidation after the South Improvement scandal, acquisitions, intimidation and negotiation, and Rockefeller’s growing dominance.
Chapter 10 — Sphinx
Lines 1298–1361. Rockefeller’s secrecy, office style, correspondence habits, self-control, and the difficulty contemporaries had in reading his motives.
Chapter 11 — The Holy Family
Lines 1362–1447. Domestic religion, children, Cettie/Laura, household rules, Baptist giving, and the intersection of family piety with business fortune.
Chapter 12 — Insurrection in the Oil Fields
Lines 1448–1579. Producer resistance, Pennsylvania oil fields, Standard Oil purchasing power, pipeline and refining politics, and anti-monopoly anger.
Chapter 13 — Seat of Empire
Lines 1580–1751. Standard Oil headquarters, New York move, national/international marketing, executive organization, and the managerial geography of empire.
Chapter 14 — The Puppeteer
Lines 1752–1933. Rockefeller’s indirect control, associates, secrecy, legal structure, pressure on independents, and the machinery of combination.
Chapter 15 — Widow’s Funeral
Lines 1934–2011. Public scandal, critics, family/business crosscurrents, and episodes that intensified suspicion of Standard Oil power.
Chapter 16 — A Matter of Trust
Lines 2012–2131. The Standard Oil Trust, trusteeship, legal innovation, capital concentration, and the trust as corporate form.
Chapter 17 — Captains of Erudition
Lines 2132–2343. Philanthropy’s intellectual organization, Frederick T. Gates, education and medicine, University of Chicago, and the shift from personal giving to expert-managed benevolence.
Chapter 18 — Nemesis
Lines 2344–2451. Ida Tarbell, Henry Demarest Lloyd, public criticism, investigative journalism, and the attack on Standard Oil’s history and legitimacy.
Chapter 19 — The Dauphin
Lines 2452–2533. John D. Rockefeller Jr.’s formation, inheritance of duty, moral burden of Standard Oil wealth, and father-son succession.
Chapter 20 — The Standard Oil Crowd
Lines 2534–2797. Rockefeller associates, internal culture, Flagler, Rogers, Archbold, and the social-business world of the Standard Oil leadership.
Chapter 21 — The Enthusiast
Lines 2798–2991. Rockefeller’s retirement-era habits, recreation, golf, estates, and the paradox of a withdrawn but still commanding public figure.
Chapter 22 — Avenging Angel
Lines 2992–3309. Progressive Era investigations, legal pressure, press hostility, Standard Oil prosecution, and the politics of antitrust.
Chapter 23 — Faith of Fools
Lines 3310–3403. Religious confidence, public defense, moral reasoning about business success, and Rockefeller’s belief in providential vindication.
Chapter 24 — The Millionaires’ Special
Lines 3404–3543. Travel, public curiosity, family movements, wealth display and restraint, and the rituals surrounding Rockefeller’s celebrity.
Chapter 25 — The Codger
Lines 3544–3657. Elderly Rockefeller as public character, dimes, jokes, staged friendliness, and controlled access to the aging oil titan.
Chapter 26 — The World’s Richest Fugitive
Lines 3658–3779. Avoidance of subpoenas and reporters, public pursuit of Rockefeller, legal vulnerability, and the spectacle of evasive wealth.
Chapter 27 — Judgment Day
Lines 3780–3937. Standard Oil antitrust judgment, breakup, Rockefeller’s reaction, and the financial consequences of dissolution.
Chapter 28 — Benevolent Trust
Lines 3938–4001. Rockefeller Foundation, philanthropy as permanent institution, medical research, public redemption, and expert-administered giving.
Chapter 29 — Massacre
Lines 4002–4151. Colorado Fuel and Iron, labor conflict, Ludlow Massacre, Rockefeller family responsibility, and the worst public-relations crisis after Standard Oil.
Chapter 30 — Introvert and Extrovert
Lines 4152–4265. Cettie’s death, Junior’s Colorado response, family grief, domestic contrast, and the father-son difference in public engagement.
Chapter 31 — Confessional
Lines 4266–4335. Late-life solitude, Florida and Pocantico habits, household companions, Inglis interviews, and controlled retrospection.
Chapter 32 — Dynastic Succession
Lines 4336–4403. John D. Rockefeller Jr. as heir, father-son reserve, transfer of responsibility, and the problem of dynastic authority.
Chapter 33 — Past, Present, Future
Lines 4404–4513. Siblings, 1919 return to boyhood landscapes, William Rockefeller, memory, Standard Oil holdings, and late family reckonings.
Chapter 34 — Heirs
Lines 4514–4597. Grandchildren, 1920s family anxieties, marriages, wealth, European allure, and problems of inheritance.
Chapter 35 — See You in Heaven
Lines 4598–4689. Final years, thrift, stock-market habits, commercialization of the Rockefeller name, death, estate, and memorial reputation.
Notes
Lines 4690–9053. Chapter notes and citations to Rockefeller papers, Inglis interviews, Tarbell, Lloyd, newspapers, memoirs, and biographies.
Acknowledgments / Bibliography
Lines 9054–9921. Research acknowledgments, bibliography, author and copyright matter.
Coverage Guide
Rockefeller and Standard Oil
Chapters 5–16 and 20–27 are the core Standard Oil material. They track the petroleum industry’s early technical and commercial setting, Cleveland refining, transport advantages, railroad rebates, the South Improvement Company, consolidation of rivals, the trust form, internal executive culture, muckraker attack, antitrust prosecution, and final dissolution. These sections should support future pages on Gilded Age technology and enterprise by contrast: Edison’s invention factory and Rockefeller’s integrated oil empire are two different models of post-Civil War industrial organization.
Industrial capitalism and antitrust politics
The book is especially strong on the debate over monopoly, government, and economic power after the Civil War. Chernow’s foreword explicitly frames Rockefeller as an embodiment of both the virtues and vices of raw American capitalism: thrift, hard work, enterprise, secrecy, coercion, and disregard for weak government boundaries.
Religion, family, and moral self-understanding
Chapters 1–4, 7, 11, 19, 23, 30–35 connect business conduct to Baptist discipline, maternal piety, household control, philanthropy, and Rockefeller’s belief that wealth and service could be reconciled. These chapters are useful for reading Rockefeller not only as a trust builder but as a religious moral actor in his own self-conception.
Muckraking and public reputation
The prelude and Chapters 18, 22, 25–27, and 31 show Rockefeller in relation to Henry Demarest Lloyd, Ida Tarbell, newspapers, legal inquiry, subpoenas, and public caricature. The material is central for Progressive Era journalism, corporate investigation, and reputation management.
Philanthropy and institution building
Chapters 17 and 28, with support from later family chapters, cover Frederick T. Gates, the University of Chicago, medical research, Rockefeller Foundation, and the shift from direct charity to expert-managed permanent institutions. This is high-value material for pages on organized philanthropy, scientific medicine, and private foundations.
Labor conflict and Ludlow
Chapter 29 and Chapter 30 cover Colorado Fuel and Iron and the Ludlow Massacre as the Rockefeller family’s major Progressive Era labor crisis. This source should be mined for a future event page on Ludlow and for a concept page on industrial relations.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 188–206: Chernow’s research framing, Rockefeller Archive Center, Inglis interviews, and the problem of treating Rockefeller as more than Standard Oil shorthand.
Lines 208–241: Rockefeller in 1917–1920 revisiting Lloyd and Tarbell, defending Standard Oil, and seeking historical vindication.
Lines 610–815: Rockefeller’s first business partnership and the move into oil refining after the Drake well and the search for cheap illuminating oil.
Lines 1020–1193: South Improvement Company, railroad rebates, oil-region revolt, and early public backlash.
Lines 2012–2131: creation and logic of the Standard Oil Trust.
Lines 2132–2343 and 3938–4001: Gates, University of Chicago, medical research, Rockefeller Foundation, and the architecture of large-scale philanthropy.
Lines 2344–2451 and 2992–3309: Tarbell, Lloyd, muckraking, Progressive legal pressure, and antitrust politics.
Lines 3780–3937: Standard Oil judgment and dissolution.
Lines 4002–4265: Colorado Fuel and Iron, Ludlow, Junior’s response, and family/public crisis.
Lines 4404–4689: 1919 return to childhood sites, late-life memory, family succession, and the afterlife of Rockefeller wealth.

Suggested Future Pages

John D. Rockefeller Sr. — entity page on Rockefeller’s business, religion, secrecy, philanthropy, public reputation, and late-life memory.
Standard Oil — entity/concept page on refining integration, transportation, trust organization, executive culture, and antitrust dissolution.
South Improvement Company — event/concept page on rebates, producer revolt, and the early anti-monopoly backlash.
Standard Oil Trust — concept page on the legal and managerial form of trust consolidation.
Ida Tarbell and Standard Oil — event/concept page on muckraking journalism and corporate investigation.
Rockefeller Philanthropy — concept page on Gates, University of Chicago, Rockefeller Foundation, medical research, and expert-administered giving.
Ludlow Massacre and the Rockefellers — event page on Colorado Fuel and Iron, labor conflict, public outrage, and Junior’s response.

Related Sources


The Wizard of Menlo Park — contrasting inventor-celebrity and laboratory-enterprise model beside Rockefeller’s oil trust and philanthropy.


A Life of George Westinghouse — contrasting engineer-industrialist and technical-corporation model beside Rockefeller’s integrated oil empire and finance.


Andrew Carnegie — steel, philanthropy, Homestead, and Carnegie as Rockefeller’s closest peer/rival in wealth and public reputation.


The House of Morgan — banking, trusts, money power, U.S. Steel, and finance-capital comparison with Standard Oil.


Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company — founder control, mass production, public reputation, and automobile capitalism beside Rockefeller’s oil system.


The Life of William McKinley, Volume II — McKinley presidency, Republican political economy, empire, and public leadership in the same late-Gilded-Age setting.


Notes on Scope
This is a late-twentieth-century secondary biography, not a contemporary source. It is valuable both for synthesis and for its source trail: Chernow uses Rockefeller family papers, the Rockefeller Archive Center, Rockefeller’s private Inglis interviews, Ida Tarbell’s files, Henry Demarest Lloyd material, Allan Nevins’s research files, newspapers, correspondence, and institutional records. Material after 1919 should be treated as legacy and afterlife rather than core chronological evidence for the 1866–1919 wiki.

sources/gates-dupont-family.title: [source] The du Pont Family (Gates, 1979)
sources/gates-dupont-family.content:
The du Pont Family
Author: John D. Gates
Published: 1979, Doubleday & Company, Garden City, N.Y. (First Edition)
Working text: PDF via pdftotext (Anna’s Archive hash 9130d08d4a9ea53ad5eca33e6890f6a5)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/gates-dupont-family.txt (pdftotext)
Extract stats: 15,031 lines · ~758 KB text
Overview
John D. Gates’s The du Pont Family is an insider’s portrait of one of America’s richest and most private industrial dynasties. Gates, a du Pont in-law for many years and a Wilmington newspaper reporter, writes from a position of unusual access: several dozen du Ponts cooperated with the project, granting interviews and opening family perspectives that earlier books had not obtained. The book is explicitly anecdotal and personal rather than strictly scholarly — Gates compares his approach to Marquis James’s biography of Alfred I. du Pont — but it covers the full sweep of the family’s American history from their landing on January 1, 1800, through the 1970s.
The first half of the book is broadly chronological: Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours’s French origins, the family’s migration to America, the founding of the gunpowder mills on Brandywine Creek, expansion into dynamite and explosives, and the transformation of the company under Pierre S. du Pont into the world’s largest chemical corporation, with holdings in General Motors, U.S. Rubber, and other industrial giants. The second half is organized by family branch — Pierre’s relatives, T. C. du Pont, Alfred I. du Pont (the “rebel”), the heirs of “the Boss,” and various other branches — before concluding with chapters on the company itself and “a way of life.”
A central narrative thread is the decline of family control. The book opens with Irenee du Pont Jr.’s 1972 letter proposing the absorption of Christiana Securities (the family holding company, which held 28.3% of Du Pont common stock) into the Du Pont Company itself — effectively ending the family’s formal control of the enterprise. The antitrust case that forced divestiture of General Motors holdings (63 million shares) and the tax and marketability pressures on Christiana are treated as the terminal phase of a dynastic arc that began with E. I. du Pont’s powder mills in 1802.
For this United States 1866–1919 wiki, the source is valuable for Gilded Age and Progressive Era industrial chemistry, the gunpowder and explosives industry, family-business governance through the holding-company form, the du Pont–GM connection, antitrust policy toward concentrated family wealth, and the social and political power of a single-family industrial empire based in a small state. Material after 1919 covers the later evolution of the company, family succession, and the 1960s–1970s dissolution of control; use those sections mainly for the long-term trajectory and afterlife of du Pont industrial power.
Narrative Source Flow
Preface
Lines 157–266. Gates explains his personal connection to the du Ponts (debutante party in 1957, marriage to a du Pont descendant, nine years as a Wilmington newspaper reporter). He contrasts his sympathetic perspective with the skeptical or hostile attitudes of fellow reporters. Describes the family’s studied avoidance of publicity and the cooperation of several dozen du Ponts in the project. Notes earlier books: Gerald Colby Zilg’s Behind the Nylon Curtain, Ralph Nader’s The Company State, Alfred Chandler and Stephen Salsbury’s Pierre S. du Pont and the Making of the Modern Corporation, and Marquis James’s Alfred I. du Pont, the Family Rebel.
Chapter 1 — Now and Then: An Overview (lines 369–1500+)
Opens with Irenee du Pont Jr.’s retirement in 1978 and the 1972 letter proposing Christiana Securities’ absorption into Du Pont.
