Christiana held 28.3% of Du Pont common stock and was the vehicle of family control; Du Pont once owned 38% of General Motors, and the 1949 antitrust suit (Attorney General Tom Clark: “the largest single concentration of industrial power in the United States”) forced GM divestiture. The chapter frames the book’s central theme: family control as a waning reality, Christiana as an albatross rather than a pendant of power, and the transformation of the du Ponts from a commanding dynasty to a dispersed, divided family.
Chapter 2 — The Move to America (lines ~1500–)
Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours (1739–1817), French physiocrat and politician, his friendship with Thomas Jefferson, the family’s escape from Revolutionary France, their arrival in Rhode Island on January 1, 1800, with one of the largest libraries ever brought to America by an immigrant family. Eleuthère Irénée du Pont’s (E. I. du Pont) decision to enter gunpowder manufacturing, the purchase of land on Brandywine Creek near Wilmington, Delaware, and the founding of the powder mills in 1802.
Chapter 3 — Building the Business (~lines –)
The early decades of the powder works, competition with established powder makers, the War of 1812 and government contracts, expansion through the nineteenth century, the introduction of dynamite and smokeless powder, and the company’s rise as the dominant American explosives manufacturer.
Chapter 4 — Two Crises (~lines –)
Two critical episodes: the powder-mill explosions that periodically devastated the Brandywine works, and the financial and operational crises that threatened the company’s survival in its early decades.
Chapter 5 — Pierre: Star of the Show (~lines –)
Pierre S. du Pont (1870–1954), the central figure of the family’s modern history. His education at MIT, his reorganization and modernization of the Du Pont Company after the 1902 crisis, the creation of the modern corporate structure, the expansion into chemicals, and the acquisition of a controlling interest in General Motors.
Chapter 6 — Two Brothers (~lines –)
Pierre’s brothers Irénée and Lammot du Pont, their roles in the company and the family, the division of responsibilities, and the dynamics of the fraternal partnership that ran Du Pont for decades.
Chapter 7 — Fathers and Sons (~lines –)
Generational relationships within the family, the pressures on du Pont sons to enter the family business, and the tension between dynastic expectation and individual ambition.
Chapter 8 — Pierre’s Other Relatives (~lines –)
The broader network of du Pont cousins and relations connected to Pierre S. du Pont’s branch, their roles in company and community, and the management of extended-family interests.
Chapter 9 — T.C. and Family (~lines –)
Thomas Coleman du Pont (T.C.), a cousin who was instrumental in the 1902 reorganization and later a U.S. Senator from Delaware. His branch’s history, political ambitions, and the 1920s conflict over family control.
Chapter 10 — The Rebel and His Relations (~lines –)
Alfred I. du Pont, the “family rebel,” who contested control after the death of the senior generation, fought legal battles over the family company, and built his own independent fortune in Florida banking and real estate.
Chapter 11 — Heirs of “the Boss” (~lines –)
The descendants of Eugene du Pont (the “Boss”), who ran the company in the late nineteenth century. Their inheritance, family position, and place in the expanded du Pont network.
Chapter 12 — A Diverse Branch (~lines –)
A lesser-known du Pont branch, their businesses and fortunes outside the main company, and the diversity of paths taken by family members.
Chapter 13 — The Underrated Victors (~lines –)
A branch of the family that built substantial independent success outside the central Du Pont Company narrative — their achievements, their relationship to the main family, and the family’s internal status hierarchies.
Chapter 14 — The In-Laws (~lines –)
The du Ponts who married into the family rather than being born into it — their roles, their acceptance (or lack thereof) in the dynastic structure, and the social dynamics of marriage into a closed wealthy family.
Chapter 15 — The Company (~lines 327–)
The Du Pont Company itself: its corporate structure, research and development, product diversification (explosives, paints, plastics, synthetic fibers — nylon, rayon, cellophane), the shift from a family-managed to a professionally-managed corporation, and the position of the family in the modern company.
Chapter 16 — A Way of Life (~lines 342–)
The social world of the du Ponts: chateaux-country estates, Wilmington society, the Brandywine landscape, charitable foundations, political influence in Delaware, and the texture of daily life in a family defined by inherited wealth and a shared name.
Appendix (~line 359 onwards)
Family charts and genealogical tables.
Coverage Guide
Gunpowder and explosives industry
Chapters 2–4 are the core material on the foundation of the du Pont powder mills, the early American gunpowder market, government contracts (War of 1812, Mexican-American War, Civil War), the transition from black powder to dynamite and smokeless powder, and the company’s quasi-monopoly position in American explosives by the late nineteenth century. This is the single most important source for the explosives and munitions side of Gilded Age industry.
Corporate reorganization and management
Chapter 5 (Pierre S. du Pont) and Chapter 15 (The Company) cover the 1902 crisis and reorganization, the creation of the modern divisional structure, scientific management, research, and diversification. Pierre S. du Pont’s MIT education and systematic approach transformed a family powder business into a diversified chemical corporation — a case study in Progressive Era corporate modernization.
Family holding company and control mechanisms
The Christiana Securities story runs through Chapters 1, 5, and 15. The family holding company as a vehicle for concentrated control, its tax advantages, the liquidity discount, the intercorporate dividends tax, and the 1972 decision to dissolve it are a unique window into dynastic wealth management in corporate form.
Antitrust, General Motors, and concentrated power
The 1949 antitrust suit (Chapter 1), the forced divestiture of 63 million GM shares, and the earlier acquisition of a 38% GM stake are central to understanding Progressive and mid-century antitrust policy toward family-controlled industrial concentrations. The du Pont–GM case is a major antitrust landmark.
Delaware and political power
The du Pont family’s relationship with Delaware — the “company state” — appears throughout the book: family members in the Senate (T.C. du Pont), governors (Pete du Pont), influence over state politics, the dominance of Wilmington by company employment and family wealth, and the broader question of concentrated private power in a small-state setting.
Family dynamics, intermarriage, and dynastic identity
Chapters 7, 14, and 16, supported by the individual branch chapters, treat the social and psychological dimensions of du Pont family life: cousin marriage (a repeated pattern), the pressure on sons to join the company, the management of reputation and publicity, and the internal status competition between branches.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 268–359: Table of contents — full chapter structure for navigation.
Lines 369–468: Chapter 1 opening — Irenee du Pont Jr.’s 1972 letter, Christiana Securities, the 1949 antitrust suit, the end of family control.
Lines 157–266: Preface — Gates’s access and perspective, the family’s cooperation, the existing literature on the du Ponts.
The Chapter 2–4 material: E. I. du Pont’s arrival, the gunpowder mills, early government contracts, and the nineteenth-century expansion of the powder business.
The Chapter 5–6 material: Pierre S. du Pont’s reorganization, the GM acquisition, and the modernization of the company.
The Chapter 15 material: the Du Pont Company as a professional-managed chemical corporation, the shift from family to management control.

Suggested Future Pages

Du Pont family — entity page on the du Pont dynasty from arrival through the 1970s, the family as an industrial and social institution.
E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company — entity/concept page on the company’s foundation, gunpowder monopoly, chemical diversification, and corporate structure.
Christiana Securities — entity/concept page on the family holding company and its role in maintaining concentrated control.
Pierre S. du Pont — entity page on the central figure of the modern Du Pont Company and his role in General Motors.
Du Pont–General Motors antitrust case — event page on the 1949 suit and forced GM divestiture.
Alfred I. du Pont — entity page on the “family rebel,” his legal battles, and his Florida ventures.

Related Sources

Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller, Sr. — contrasting model of dynastic industrial wealth: a single-founder oil trust vs. a multi-generational family chemical company.
The House of Morgan — banking and finance-capital dynastic comparison: Morgan’s partnership model vs. du Pont’s family-corporation model.
Andrew Carnegie — steel wealth and philanthropic institutionalization as a contrasting Gilded Age fortune: single founder, no dynastic continuity.
The First Tycoon: The Epic Life of Cornelius Vanderbilt — early nineteenth-century dynastic foundation vs. du Pont’s longer arc from 1800 through the twentieth century.

Notes on Scope
This is a late-twentieth-century popular biography by an insider, not an academic monograph. It is anecdotal and personal in approach and largely sympathetic to the family. Its value lies in the access Gates obtained — interviews with several dozen du Ponts — and in its comprehensive sweep from 1800 to the 1970s. For this 1866–1919 wiki, the core chapters are 2–5 (business foundation and reorganization) and the early portions of 1, 15, and 16 (company structure and family control). Later chapters covering the 1920s–1970s are useful mainly for the long-term arc of dynastic decline and the antitrust aftermath.

sources/lindbergh-banking-currency-money.title: [source] Banking and Currency and the Money Trust (Lindbergh, 1913)
sources/lindbergh-banking-currency-money.content:
Banking and Currency and the Money Trust
Author: Charles A. Lindbergh Sr.
Published: National Capital Press, Washington, D.C., copyright 1913
Working text: Hathi/IA-style OCR ZIP via Anna’s Archive (oclc 2313532, hash ec19b274f791503ed98837980ebd97e9)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/lindbergh-banking-currency-money-trust.txt
Extract stats: 328 OCR page files · 10,311 lines · ~75,605 words · 436,392 bytes
Completeness Assessment
The OCR ZIP appears complete as a compact single-volume work. The joined raw text includes title and copyright pages, a contents page, the full sequence of named sections from General Observations through The Practical Side of a Better Financial System, and Appendices A–B.
Overview
Lindbergh writes as a Progressive-era critic of concentrated finance during the public controversy over the Money Trust and banking reform. He argues that commodity prices, bank credit, interest, dividends, rent, and short selling are shaped less by natural production and demand than by a manipulated money system controlled by Wall Street financiers. The book is valuable for this wiki as a near-contemporary polemic against the financial order just before the Federal Reserve Act, and as a bridge between Populist-style monetary criticism, Progressive regulation, congressional investigation, and wartime-era anti-finance politics.
The source pairs directly with Why Is Your Country at War? because Lindbergh later presents the 1917 war crisis as a continuation of the conditions he attacked in 1913. It should also be mined alongside The House of Morgan for the institutional finance side of the same debates and Recent History of the United States for the broader context of banking reform, the 1907 panic, Aldrich-Vreeland, and Progressive politics.
Narrative Source Flow
Front Matter and Contents
Lines 1–116. The title and copyright pages identify Lindbergh as author and National Capital Press as publisher. The contents page lays out the source as a sequence of practical political-economy arguments: general observations, introduction, diagnosis, banking/currency/Money Trust, interest and rents, short selling, political aspects, deposit guarantees, money, remedies, and appendices.
General Observations
Lines 118–206. Lindbergh begins from the claim that material production and consumption are relatively stable, while market prices and commercial relations fluctuate sharply because of human institutions. He frames banking and currency reform, industrial relations, and political reform as connected problems created by a money system that makes the people subordinate to concentrated financial power.
Introduction and In Contemplation
Lines 207–709. The opening argument presents the money problem as the first of several linked studies in business, politics, and social relations. Lindbergh attacks inherited financial habits, asks readers to examine who benefits from existing credit arrangements, and argues that public credit should serve the people rather than private financial groups.
What Is the Matter with Us?
Lines 710–914. This section poses the book’s diagnosis in direct political language: the problem is not merely technical banking procedure but a social order in which common productive capacity is turned into claims for private tribute. It is useful for future pages on Progressive monetary critique, popular anti-monopoly thought, and the political language of financial reform.
Currency, Banking, and the Money Trust
Lines 915–4276. This is the central section. Lindbergh discusses bank organization, national-bank capital, reserves, deposits, credit creation, stock ownership, clearing-house power, Wall Street influence, and congressional inquiry into the Money Trust. He treats the banking system as a political institution that permits a small group to expand or contract credit and thereby shape markets, production, and livelihoods.
Interest, Dividends and Rents; Short Selling
Lines 4277–5191. Lindbergh extends the critique from banks to claims on production. Interest, dividends, rents, watered stock, and speculative short selling are presented as mechanisms that transfer the fruits of labor and production to non-producing claimants. The short-selling section is especially useful for the source’s view of speculative markets as a form of social control rather than ordinary commerce.
Political Aspect, Bank Guarantees, and Money
Lines 5192–6010. These sections move from economic diagnosis to political remedy. Lindbergh discusses the relation between financial power and party politics, government guarantee of bank deposits, the meaning of money, and the way gold and credit acquire value through public authority.
The Remedy, Two-Fold Remedy, and Practical System
Lines 6011–8818. Lindbergh proposes a replacement system in which the public, through government, controls credit rather than leaving monetary power to private banks. This long remedy section should be mined for concrete proposals, including his distinction between a moral-political remedy and the practical machinery of a better financial system.
Appendices A–B
Lines 8819–10311. Appendix A responds to reader questions and includes correspondence and discussion bearing on banking reform. Appendix B reproduces excerpts from Lindbergh’s arguments before the House Rules Committee and House debate connected to the campaign for a special Money Trust investigation.
Coverage Guide
Use this source for Progressive-era banking and currency politics, Money Trust rhetoric, critiques of Wall Street, public-credit proposals, and the intellectual background to congressional banking reform. It is less a neutral manual of banking than a political-economic pamphlet from inside the reform fight; claims about institutions should be cross-checked against banking histories and congressional material before becoming entity-page facts.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 60–72: Lindbergh’s prefatory thesis that daily price fluctuations prove manipulation by the Money Trust.
Lines 147–187: banking/currency, industrial relations, and political reform stated as connected public problems.
Lines 915–4276: main treatment of national banks, reserves, deposits, credit, and the Money Trust.
Lines 4998–5191: short selling as a condensed example of his critique of speculative markets.
Lines 5192–6010: financial power, party politics, deposit guarantees, and the meaning of money.
Lines 8819–10311: appendices tying the book to reader questions and Lindbergh’s congressional Money Trust investigation campaign.

Suggested Future Pages

Money Trust — concept/entity page on Progressive-era descriptions of concentrated financial power.
Banking Reform and the Federal Reserve Act — event/concept page linking Lindbergh, the 1907 panic, Aldrich-Vreeland, Wilson, and the Federal Reserve.
Charles A. Lindbergh Sr. — entity page covering his congressional role, anti-Money Trust politics, and 1917 war critique.
Progressive Monetary Reform — concept page connecting banking, currency, credit, farm-labor politics, and anti-monopoly ideas.

Related Sources

Why Is Your Country at War? — Lindbergh’s 1917 extension of his anti-finance critique into wartime politics.
The House of Morgan — banking-house and international finance context for the institutions Lindbergh opposed.
Recent History of the United States — broader synthesis of banking reform, Progressive politics, and the Federal Reserve era.

Notes on Scope
This is a polemical reform source written by an active political critic. It is strongest as evidence for Lindbergh’s own anti-Money Trust argument and for Progressive-era monetary language; it should not be treated as a neutral institutional account without corroborating sources.

sources/lindbergh-why-is-your-country-at.title: [source] Why Is Your Country at War and What Happens to You after the War (Lindbergh, 1917)
sources/lindbergh-why-is-your-country-at.content:
Why Is Your Country at War and What Happens to You after the War
Author: Charles A. Lindbergh Sr.
Published: National Capital Press, Washington, D.C., copyright 1917
Working text: Hathi/IA-style OCR ZIP via Anna’s Archive (oclc 4960650, hash 304536f6009bdfe984f4d19bbd722394)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/lindbergh-why-is-your-country-at-war.txt
Extract stats: 228 OCR page files · 8,491 lines · ~67,955 words · 383,578 bytes
Completeness Assessment
The OCR ZIP appears complete as a single-volume wartime pamphlet/book. The joined raw text includes cover/title material, copyright page, introductory notice, chapters II–VIII as marked in the OCR, and an index. Chapter I appears to be represented by the unnumbered Introductory opening rather than by a visible CHAPTER I heading in the OCR.
Overview
Lindbergh writes after the United States entered World War I. He states support for the United States once Congress and the President have acted, but argues that the country was brought to war by prewar economic and political conditions rather than by the war alone. His central claim is that a financial and business “inner circle” shaped public opinion, press narratives, and national policy in ways that made violation of American rights and war increasingly likely.
For this wiki, the source is valuable because it captures a 1917 dissenting Progressive-era argument about war, finance, party politics, and democratic sovereignty from a former congressman already known for anti-Money Trust agitation. It should be read with Banking and Currency and the Money Trust as the continuation of Lindbergh’s 1913 critique, with Recent History of the United States for the broader World War I narrative, and with The House of Morgan for wartime finance and Anglo-American banking connections.
Narrative Source Flow
Front Matter and Reader Notice
Lines 1–143. The cover and title pages identify the book as Why Is Your Country at War and What Happens to You after the War and Related Subjects, published in Washington in 1917. Lindbergh explicitly connects the new wartime book to his 1913 Banking and Currency and the Money Trust, saying the conditions he predicted in that earlier work are now taking place.
Introductory Opening / Implied Chapter I
Lines 144–291. Lindbergh asks readers to consider the war crisis as part of a larger failure of existing civilization and of the “old order of things.” He argues that the war is not the largest problem itself; rather, the conditions that existed before the war and caused entry into it must be solved or they will lead to further wars. He denies that criticism before and after official action is disloyal, while insisting that once the nation is at war Americans must support the United States in real necessity.
Chapter II — Possession of the Earth: What For?
Lines 292–399. This chapter frames war and social conflict through rights to the earth, possession, labor, domination, and industrial slavery. Lindbergh uses broad moral-political language to ask why mankind fights over advantages and why claims of rule and possession lead to destructive conflict.
Chapter III — Continental and Political Environments in America
Lines 400–630. Lindbergh emphasizes the United States’ continental position and political opportunity. He argues that America’s geography and republican institutions should have allowed a better social order, but that domestic and international rights have been neglected while concentrated interests gained control.
Chapter IV — The Exploiters
Lines 631–770. This chapter attacks public celebration of big-business figures as “builders” and recasts them as exploiters. It is useful for tracing Lindbergh’s anti-monopoly language, his suspicion of press and magazine influence, and his effort to separate actual production from financial or corporate command over production.
Chapter V — You—Yourself
Lines 771–1615. Lindbergh addresses farmers, wage workers, and productive citizens directly. He asks why capital, itself produced by labor, should sit above labor as master. The section is rich for future pages on farmer-labor politics, popular political economy, and Progressive-era rhetoric of sovereignty and production.
Chapter VI — The Farmer and Wall Street Speculator after Emergency Currency
Lines 1616–2160. This chapter is presented as a dialogue. A politician, speculator, and farmer discuss emergency currency, the Federal Reserve banking system, speculation, and the relation between Wall Street and agricultural producers. The dialogue format makes it a compact dramatization of Lindbergh’s view that emergency monetary machinery favored speculators over farmers.
Chapter VII — Memorial to the Presidents
Lines 2161–5633. The longest chapter is a memorial-style appeal to national leadership. It ranges across patriotism, democratic authority, banking, war, industrial order, political corruption, citizenship, and the rights of Americans. This section should be mined selectively for Lindbergh’s proposed reform program and his language about official authority versus sovereign citizenship.
Chapter VIII — The Political Parties
Lines 5634–8245. Lindbergh closes the narrative by criticizing party loyalty and arguing that dominant parties no longer serve their originating purposes. The chapter is useful for pages on Progressive-era party realignment, insurgency, third-party thought, and critiques of machine or boss politics during the war period.
Index
Lines 8246–8491. The index gives useful entry points into recurring subjects such as American rights, autocratic power, banking, currency, farmers, political parties, press influence, speculation, and war.
Coverage Guide
Use this source for wartime dissent, Progressive anti-finance politics, criticism of press and business influence, farmer-labor monetary critique, and the connection Lindbergh drew between domestic political economy and World War I. It is not a general military history of the war; its value lies in explaining how a particular anti-Money Trust politician interpreted America’s entry into war and the postwar consequences he expected.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 104–137: explicit link back to Banking and Currency and the Money Trust and Lindbergh’s claim that the earlier diagnosis had been confirmed.
Lines 144–291: opening statement on war, patriotism, criticism, press accusations, and the claim that prewar conditions caused the war crisis.
Lines 190–205: claim that an unauthorized “inner circle” maneuvered conditions toward war.
Lines 631–770: critique of big-business men as exploiters rather than builders.
Lines 1616–2160: dialogue on emergency currency, the Federal Reserve system, Wall Street speculation, and farmers.
Lines 5634–8245: critique of the dominant political parties and wartime party loyalty.

Suggested Future Pages

Charles A. Lindbergh Sr. — entity page linking congressional anti-Money Trust work, 1913 banking critique, and 1917 wartime dissent.
American Entry into World War I — event page contrasting official causes, neutrality, submarine warfare, finance, and dissenting critiques.
Wartime Dissent in the United States — concept page on criticism, loyalty, press pressure, and citizen rights after U.S. entry into the war.
Farmer-Labor Monetary Politics — concept page connecting farmers, wage workers, emergency currency, speculation, and banking reform.

Related Sources

Banking and Currency and the Money Trust — the 1913 financial critique that Lindbergh says underlies his 1917 wartime argument.
Recent History of the United States — broader near-contemporary synthesis for neutrality, preparedness, war government, and peace.
The House of Morgan — wartime finance, international banking, and Morgan-connected war loans.

Notes on Scope
This is a polemical wartime source by a critic of concentrated finance and war policy. It should be used as direct evidence for Lindbergh’s interpretation and for domestic dissenting rhetoric in 1917, not as a standalone explanation of all causes of American entry into World War I.

sources/nevins-ford-times-man-company.title: [source] Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company (Nevins, 1954)
sources/nevins-ford-times-man-company.content:
Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company
Author: Allan Nevins, with the collaboration of Frank Ernest Hill
Published: Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1954
Working text: Hathi-style OCR ZIP via Anna’s Archive (oclc 14396135, hash 6f98059656bb5ee5aab85ffe0af25ec3)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/nevins-ford-times-man-company.txt (joined OCR page text with page markers)
Extract stats: 778 OCR page files · 33,690 lines · ~311,503 words · 1,852,624 bytes
Completeness Assessment
The source appears complete as a usable OCR text. The ZIP contains 778 page .txt files sorting naturally from 00000001.txt through 00000778.txt; the joined raw file includes front matter, title/copyright pages, preface, full contents, illustrations list, all twenty-two chapters, notes, ten appendices, bibliography, and index. There are expected OCR artifacts and some blank or image-caption pages, but the book structure is intact and the final pages continue through the index rather than stopping mid-text.
This is the first volume of the Nevins/Hill Ford history, so it is complete as this volume rather than as the whole Ford story. Its chronological endpoint is the company and Ford by roughly 1916–1918, with Chapter XXII explicitly focused on rising dangers in Ford’s character, advisers, and autocratic control. That scope fits the United States 1866–1919 wiki especially well.
Overview
Nevins frames the automobile not as an isolated invention but as part of a deeper transformation in roads, transport, mechanical skill, factory organization, and American mass production. The preface says the book is simultaneously a history of Ford Motor Company, a partial biography of Henry Ford, and a broader history of the early automotive industry. It draws heavily on Ford Motor Company Archives, oral histories, Detroit Public Library collections, University of Michigan materials, legal records, trade periodicals, and contemporary newspapers.
For this wiki, the source is central for Henry Ford, Detroit, the automobile industry, mass production, Model T, Ford Motor Company, the Selden patent case, labor welfare policy, the five-dollar day, and the transformation of industrial work before World War I. It pairs naturally with The Wizard of Menlo Park for Edison and inventor-celebrity context, with A Life of George Westinghouse for machinery and industrial technology, with The House of Morgan for finance-capital and corporate consolidation, and with Andrew Carnegie for comparison between steel-era and automobile-era industrial organization.
Narrative Source Flow
Preface
Lines 60–164. Nevins defines the book as a Ford Motor Company history, an automotive-industry history, and a partial biography of Henry Ford. He emphasizes that motor cars and automobile factories transformed modern economic and social life, explains Columbia University’s independent role in the project, and identifies the Ford Archives and oral histories as major source foundations.
Chapter I — The Road: The Wheel
Lines 699–1531. The opening chapter places the automobile in the long American struggle to conquer distance. It moves from trails, packhorses, crude roads, wagons, canals, and railroads to the neglected condition of rural roads, making the modern highway and motor car appear as solutions to a national transport problem rather than as sudden novelties.
Chapter II — The Pioneers
Lines 1532–2216. Nevins introduces early automotive pioneers such as the Duryeas, Haynes, Olds, and Winton, then turns to Henry Ford’s birth near Dearborn during the Civil War. The chapter roots Ford in Irish immigrant, Michigan frontier, and Nowlin/Ford family settings, treating pioneer conditions as part of the mental world that shaped later mechanical ambition.
Chapter III — The Childhood of an Industrialist
Lines 2217–2958. This chapter connects Ford’s childhood to Detroit and the machine age rising in the Midwest. It covers William and Mary Ford, farm holdings, Ford’s siblings, school life, early mechanical experiments, and especially the influence of Mary Ford before her death in 1876.
Chapter IV — Youth and the Machines
Lines 2959–3786. Ford’s encounter with a portable steam engine becomes the chapter’s central awakening. Nevins broadens from Ford’s watch-repair skill and the 1876 Centennial Exposition to the history of steam and gas engines, Lenoir, Otto, Brayton, and Ford’s decision to leave farm life for Detroit in 1879.
Chapter V — A Persistent Apprentice
Lines 3787–4539. The young Ford enters industrial Detroit through the Michigan Car Company, the Flower brothers, Detroit Drydock, watch repair, stationary engines, Westinghouse engine work, and business college. The chapter makes Detroit’s shop culture and Ford’s persistent apprenticeship the bridge between farm youth and automotive experimentation.
Chapter VI — The Broadening Stream
Lines 4540–5660. Nevins widens the field to steam, gas, gasoline, the four-cycle engine, Siegfried Marcus, George B. Selden, Daimler, Benz, and other European and American developments. Ford’s courtship and marriage to Clara Bryant, sawmill work, engine repair, and decision to return to Detroit place him inside a growing international stream of road-carriage experiment.
Chapter VII — The Eve of Revolution
Lines 5661–6644. Ford works as night engineer at Edison Illuminating Company while Detroit becomes a more favorable industrial center. The chapter follows Daimler, Benz, Panhard & Levassor, Roger, Duryea, Olds, Haynes, Maxim, and early races in France and Chicago, showing that Ford’s experiments occurred amid accelerating transatlantic automotive activity.
Chapter VIII — A Horseless Carriage
Lines 6645–7800. Ford builds and runs his quadricycle in 1896 after experiments with small engines and help from Charles B. King, Barthel, Cato, Bishop, and Huff. The chapter compares Ford’s work with Duryea, Haynes, Olds, Winton, and Edison’s encouragement, ending with Ford selling the quadricycle and beginning a new car.
Chapter IX — Time of Experiment
Lines 7801–8771. Ford seeks backers, demonstrates a new car, and forms the Detroit Automobile Company while leaving Edison Illuminating. Nevins follows local support from William C. Maybury and William H. Murphy, the company’s failure in 1900, the bicycle’s influence on car manufacture, and Ford’s shift toward racing as a way to recover reputation.
Chapter X — Racing: A Prelude
Lines 8772–10089. Ford’s 1901 race against Winton, the Henry Ford Company, conflict with Murphy, Henry M. Leland’s role, Ford’s withdrawal, Tom Cooper, Barney Oldfield, and the new racer all make racing a prelude to the final company. The chapter shows reputation, publicity, family life, and investor confidence converging before Ford Motor Company.
Chapter XI — The Ford Motor Company
Lines 10090–11875. Nevins narrates Ford’s association with Alexander Malcomson, Harold Wills, James Couzens, the Dodge Brothers, John S. Gray, and the investors who formed Ford Motor Company with only $28,000 paid in. Model A, early bankruptcy risk, dealers, Couzens’s office role, Ford’s technical role, demand, defects, and first dividends define the company’s first success.
Chapter XII — A Battle for the Cheap Car
Lines 11876–13207. Ford battles internally for a light, inexpensive car against Malcomson’s preference for higher-priced models. The chapter covers Detroit’s automotive rise, good roads, Models A and B, Piquette Avenue, Galamb, Sorensen, Seeman, Emde, dealer growth, the Ford Manufacturing Company maneuver, and the stockholder struggle that secured the cheap-car strategy.
Chapter XIII — The Shadow of Monopoly
Lines 13208–15003. The Selden patent case dominates the chapter. Nevins explains the Electric Vehicle Company, Association of Licensed Automobile Manufacturers, Ford’s rebuffed licensing request, R. A. Parker’s advice to fight, Ford’s advertising counterattack, legal evidence, the Selden buggy, the Ford-Lenoir car, and the propaganda war around automotive monopoly.
Chapter XIV — Forerunner: Model N
Lines 15004–16321. The Model N gives Ford a sturdy, low-priced success before Model T. The chapter covers Malcomson’s surrender, Couzens’s acquisition of stock, merger of Ford Manufacturing and Ford Motor Company, Norval Hawkins’s sales role, Ford’s racing interests, vanadium steel, and planning for a still cheaper car.
Chapter XV — New Growth, New Problems
Lines 16322–17828. The panic of 1907, weak-firm failures, Highland Park planning, Canadian and British expansion, Percival Perry, H. B. White in Europe, P. E. Martin and Charles Sorensen in manufacturing, labor conditions in Detroit, antiunion employers, I.W.W. activity, and Ford plant working conditions frame the company just before Model T’s ascent.
Chapter XVI — The Advent of Model T
Lines 17829–19059. Model T receives its central chapter: advance publicity, Ford, Galamb, Wills, experimental-room work, vanadium steel, transmission, magneto, carburetor, bearings, tires, branches, dealers, service, the New York-Seattle race, branch assembly plants, British success, and Durant’s proposed merger into what became General Motors.
Chapter XVII — No Monopoly
Lines 19060–20481. The Selden patent battle reaches judgment and appeal. Judge Hough first supports the patent, the A.L.A.M. celebrates, Ford appeals, Judge Walter C. Noyes delivers a decision favorable to Ford, license payments stop, the industry is freed for broader activity, Ford buys the Keim plant, and the Ford and Couzens families adjust to wealth.
Chapter XVIII — A Lever to Move the World
Lines 20482–21848. Highland Park and mass production become the chapter’s subject. Nevins follows the move to the plant, building and machinery layout, Keim Mills, Knudsen, Smith, Lee, sequential production, conveyor belts, magneto/engine/chassis assemblies, Clarence Avery, 1912–1917 output gains, the Dodge contract break, and full adaptation to mass production.
Chapter XIX — The Anatomy of Success
Lines 21849–23240. Nevins analyzes the elements of Ford’s success: modernization of automobiles, self-starters, lights, left-hand drive, roads and license/gasoline revenues, the Lincoln Highway, Model T price cuts, parts service, mass-production economies, young executives, branch assembly, process improvement, sales organization, and the 1914 reduction to a $440 basic car.
Chapter XX — The Five-Dollar Day
Lines 23241–24529. The chapter places Ford’s 1914 wage announcement inside national labor conditions, declining unionism, the Employers’ Association of Detroit, immigrant labor supply, John R. Lee’s wage system, profit-sharing experiments, swelling profits, public praise and criticism, and debates over whether Ford, Couzens, Clara Ford, or Percival Perry shaped the measure.
Chapter XXI — The Company and the Worker
Lines 24530–25724. Nevins follows the immediate rush of job applicants, eligibility rules, women and clerical workers, labor costs, morale, beneficial services, wartime/living-cost complications, the Sociological Department, home investigations, criticism of privacy invasion, and Ford policies toward handicapped workers, ex-criminals, adjustment, and advancement.
Chapter XXII — Rising Dangers
Lines 25725–26572. The final chapter covers 1915–1916 production increases, price cuts, Ford at fifty-three, his dynamic philosophy, the end of the Dodge contract, operating committees, Edsel, the shift toward absolute personal power, Ford’s mechanical brilliance, intellectual limits, aloofness, inconsistent judgment outside his field, and danger from weaker advisers.
Notes, Appendices, Bibliography, and Index
Lines 26573–33690. The back matter is substantial. Notes run chapter by chapter; appendices preserve supporting evidence such as Ford family genealogy, production/sales/materials data, early stockholders, branch organization, and fiscal figures; the bibliography describes Ford Archives, oral histories, Detroit Public Library, University of Michigan, and related source collections; the index runs to the final OCR pages.
Coverage Guide
Automobiles, roads, and the American transport problem
Chapters I, VI, VII, and VIII connect the automobile to older road, wagon, canal, railroad, steam, gas-engine, and gasoline traditions. This source can support future pages on roads, good-roads reform, early automobiles, and the shift from railroad-dominated transport to motorized mobility.
Henry Ford and Ford Motor Company
Chapters II–XII provide the core biography and company-formation arc: Dearborn origins, farm childhood, Detroit apprenticeship, Edison Illuminating, the quadricycle, failed companies, racing, Malcomson, Couzens, Wills, the Dodges, Model A, and the victory of the cheap-car strategy. These chapters are the foundation for future Henry Ford and Ford Motor Company entity pages.
Patent monopoly and industry freedom
Chapters XIII and XVII are the main Selden patent sections. They connect legal strategy, Ford advertising, A.L.A.M. power, court evidence, Judge Hough, Judge Noyes, and the freeing of the industry from a licensing regime.
Mass production and Highland Park
Chapters XVI–XIX are the key mass-production cluster. They cover Model T, Highland Park, Keim Mills, conveyor belts, component assembly, process synchronization, branch assembly, price reductions, and the managerial/technical team behind Ford’s output gains.
Labor policy and Progressive Era industrial welfare
Chapters XX and XXI are the strongest labor sections: the five-dollar day, immigrant labor, Detroit employer associations, profit-sharing, welfare work, Sociological Department home investigations, and Ford’s attempt to link wages, morality, stability, and production.
Character, autocracy, and future risk
Chapter XXII is the interpretive pivot at the end of the volume. It presents Ford as mechanically brilliant and commercially successful, but increasingly autocratic, aloof, and vulnerable to poor advisers and unsound judgments outside his practical field.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 60–164: Nevins’s preface on scope, Columbia independence, Ford Archives, oral histories, and the automobile factory as mass-production revolution.
Lines 699–1531: road history and transport as a national American problem before the automobile.
Lines 3787–4539: Detroit apprenticeship, Detroit Drydock, Westinghouse engine work, and Ford’s mechanical formation.
Lines 5661–7800: Edison Illuminating, Charles B. King, the quadricycle, early gasoline-car context, and Edison’s encouragement.
Lines 10090–11875: founding of Ford Motor Company, Model A, Couzens/Ford work division, dealers, first dividends.
Lines 13208–15003 and 19060–20481: Selden patent conflict, A.L.A.M., trial, appeal, and industry-wide consequences.
Lines 17829–21848: Model T, Highland Park, vanadium steel, moving assembly, conveyor belts, and mass-production synchronization.
Lines 23241–25724: five-dollar day, labor policy, Sociological Department, welfare supervision, and worker relations.
Lines 30077–30645 and following bibliography pages: source trail for Ford Archives, oral histories, Detroit Public Library, University of Michigan, trade periodicals, and automotive records.

Suggested Future Pages

Henry Ford — entity page on Dearborn origins, mechanical apprenticeship, racing, company building, Model T, labor policy, and autocratic control.
Ford Motor Company — entity page on investors, early models, cheap-car strategy, dealer network, Highland Park, Model T, and mass production.
Model T — concept/entity page on design, low price, vanadium steel, service network, and American mobility.
Highland Park Plant — entity/concept page on plant layout, moving assembly, sequential production, and process synchronization.
Five-Dollar Day — event/concept page on the 1914 wage announcement, eligibility rules, public reaction, and labor-welfare system.
Selden Patent Case — event/concept page on automotive patent monopoly, Ford resistance, A.L.A.M., and the 1911 appeal.
Mass Production in the United States — concept page linking Ford, Carnegie steel, Edison/Westinghouse electrical systems, and Progressive Era industrial organization.

Related Sources


The Wizard of Menlo Park — Edison, Edison Illuminating, inventor publicity, and Ford’s later relationship to Edison.


A Life of George Westinghouse — machinery, engines, industrial technology, and Westinghouse Engine work in Ford’s apprenticeship.


Andrew Carnegie — comparison for mass industrial organization, labor policy, and the passage from steel capitalism to automobile capitalism.


The House of Morgan — financial and corporate-capital context for the era of industrial consolidation in which Ford resisted merger and outside control.


Titan — comparison for founder control, corporate organization, public reputation, and industrial wealth.


The Life of William McKinley, Volume II — McKinley’s final speech on commerce, transportation, communications, reciprocity, foreign markets, and the end of isolation.


Notes on Scope
This is a company-sponsored but Columbia-administered modern secondary history with heavy archival use. It should be mined as a major source for early Ford and automotive industry history through the 1910s, while remembering that it is Volume I of a larger Ford project and not the full late-life story of Henry Ford.

sources/nevins-hill-ford-expansion-1915-.title: [source] Ford: Expansion and Challenge, 1915–1933 (Nevins & Hill, 1957)
sources/nevins-hill-ford-expansion-1915-.content:
Ford: Expansion and Challenge, 1915–1933
Author: Allan Nevins and Frank Ernest Hill
Research associates: William Greenleaf and George B. Heliker
Published: Charles Scribner’s Sons, New York, 1957
Working text: Internet Archive PDF via Anna’s Archive (hash bfcc9c354be4fc003f49da999c3c9d28; IA fordexpansionchaOOalla)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/nevins-hill-ford-expansion-1915-1933.txt (pdftotext -layout)
Extract stats: 30,920 lines · ~312,489 words · 1,982,917 bytes
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1920-45 into the United States 1866–1919 wiki because Volume II opens in 1915 and covers material through U.S. participation in World War I. Its strongest overlap with this folder is Chapters I–V (and related war chapters): Panama-Pacific / Highland Park 1915, the Peace Ship, wartime production, Wilson support in 1916, and the wartime political forays. Post-1919 material (Rouge as colossus, Dearborn Independent campaign peak, Model T’s end, Model A, early Depression) remains primarily for the 1920–45 wiki. Pair with Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company (Volume I) already in this wiki.
Completeness Assessment
The source appears complete as a usable OCR text of the full second volume. Front matter includes the Internet Archive digitize stamp, title page (Expansion and Challenge 1915–1933), Scribner’s imprint, 1957 copyright (Allan Nevins; A-7-57[V]), LC card 57-9695, Preface, Contents (chs. I–XXIII plus Notes, Appendices, Bibliographical Note, Index), and Illustrations list. Body text runs from Chapter I through XXIII; notes begin near line 26,244 with chapter-keyed citations; appendices and index follow through the final pages. OCR is noisy on early cover/scan pages (roughly lines 1–68) and shows hyphenation, character substitution, and occasional running-header garble, but chapter structure and continuous narrative are intact.
This is Volume II of the Columbia University / Ford Motor Company Fund trilogy. Volume I (Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company, 1954) ends near the five-dollar day and the rise of personal power (covered in the United States 1866–1919 wiki). Volume III (Ford: Decline and Rebirth, 1933–1962) continues from the New Deal crisis through Henry Ford II and corporate rebirth.
Overview
The preface frames 1915–1933 as the years when Ford Motor Company released “powerful new forces in American life”: mass production perfected at Highland Park, Model T as the most widely used vehicle in human history, the River Rouge as vertical integration (mines, forests, foundries, steel, glass, railroad, fleets), airplane and tractor ventures, overseas plants, and the socio-economic experimentation of high wages and inexpensive goods even as Henry Ford became an industrial autocrat. The volume is the product of the same Columbia–Ford Fund arrangement as Volume I: written under university auspices, university employees and salaries, royalties to Columbia, authors’ independence guaranteed; Columbia takes no responsibility for content.
For this United States 1866–1919 wiki, mine first the 1915–1919 overlap (Peace Ship, war production, Wilson years); the full war–boom–depression arc is central in the 1920–45 copy. The source covers Henry Ford and Edsel Ford in war, boom, and depression; Ford Motor Company organization and one-man rule; Rouge construction; Model T’s climax and death; Model A and the V-8 transition; the Peace Ship; wartime production and the unreturned war-profits pledge; the Dodge minority suit and buy-out; the Dearborn Independent and anti-Semitism; Muscle Shoals; labor after the Sociological Department’s idealistic phase; Harry Bennett’s rise; and Ford overseas in the expansive and nationalist years. It pairs with Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company (vol. 1) and Ford: Decline and Rebirth, 1933–1962 (vol. 3), and with contemporary narrative sources such as Only Yesterday and Since Yesterday.
Narrative Source Flow
Preface
Lines 130–240 approx. Nevins and Hill date the story from Woodrow Wilson’s reelection through war, boom, and into the Great Depression. Ford by 1915 already ranked among major world industrials and was making Americans an automobile-using people. Expansion includes mass production’s full instrument at Highland Park, Model T’s ubiquity, Rouge vertical integration, airplanes and tractors, overseas plants, and the challenge that ends Model T. Socio-economic experimentation in wages and sales advances and retreats; Ford believes in high wages and abundant cheap goods while becoming an autocrat. Volume I covered beginnings through the Five Dollar Day and dawn of mass production (1913–14); this volume covers war, boom, and incipient depression under the Columbia–Ford Fund independence arrangement. Acknowledgment of Ford Archives (Dr. Henry Edmunds), Owen Bombard’s oral-history interviews, and research associates Greenleaf and Heliker.
Chapter I — Scene and Actors: 1915
Lines 639–1654. Opens at the Panama-Pacific Exposition, 20 February 1915: Ford’s Highland Park assembly-line replica draws crowds until rails fail and the line is shut to restore order. Mass production is unveiled; the line later turns out twenty cars a day for nine months. Context: Panama Canal (August 1914), world war mechanization, continental telephone and wireless, skyscraper height debate. Survey of the United States as industrial power; the automotive industry’s social and technological influence; Highland Park as mass-production exemplar; Henry Ford’s associates, friends, and interests—world peace, the tractor, and a projected manufacturing center on the River Rouge.
Chapter II — Peace Crusade
Lines 1655–2856. Ford’s peace activity from November 1915: Rosika Schwimmer and Louis P. Lochner; continuous mediation; interview with Wilson; Clara Ford won to the cause; telegram barrage. The Oscar II peace ship, sensationalism, haste, poor planning, ridicule and defenders; quarrel among pilgrims; Ford leaves the cruise in Norway but supports a European commission until American entry into the war ends the effort.
Chapter III — Producing for War
Lines 2857–4184. Ford’s shift from peace advocate to war supporter after the break with Germany (February 1917) and declaration of war: plants offered without profit; tractors for Britain then America; ambulances, helmets, shells, armor plate; Liberty engine work; Eagle boat submarine chasers on the Rouge; tank experiments. Attacks on personnel including Edsel and Carl Emde. Promise to return war profits, controversy, and eventual failure to repay.
Chapter IV — Drive for Power
Lines 4185–5362. Edsel’s marriage (November 1916) and the Dodge brothers’ suit the next day to stop expansion spending and force a large special dividend. Trial: Ford as colorful witness; court-ordered dividend over $19,000,000. Ford holds 58½ percent yet is not free to direct policy; threat of a new car depresses stock; secret purchase of all minority holdings. Immense personal power and plans for using it.
Chapter V — Forays in Politics
Lines 5363–6542. Support for Wilson in 1916 (perhaps crucial). 1918 Michigan senatorial race as Democrat; defeat by Newberry and investigations. Dearborn Independent launched 1920 as liberal weekly. Chicago Tribune suit over “anarchist” / “ignorant idealist” editorial; Ford’s humiliation as witness; press comment and public standing.
Chapter VI — Postwar Crisis
Lines 6543–7698. Industry’s war-to-peace transition; retooling; loss of Wills, Lee, and Hawkins. Boom production slowed by strikes then collapsed with the postwar bust. September 1920 price cut fails to hold demand; plant shutdowns; surplus equipment sold; organization simplified. Need for funds to repay the minority-stock loan; defiance of bankers; plant reopening and shipment of cars to dealers (February–March 1921). Crisis met; production mounts; discharge of officials including Knudsen and Klingensmith.
Chapter VII — The Lincoln Story
Lines 7699–8926. Lincoln Motor Company crisis, fall 1921; Henry M. and Wilfred Leland; receivership; Edsel’s interest; Ford acquisition at receiver’s sale; clash with Lelands and their departure; payment of old creditors; 1927 Leland suit for former stockholders lost; appraisal of Ford’s role.
Chapter VIII — The Rouge: Concept and Growth
Lines 8927–9565. Ford’s new efficiency conception, 1918–1924: control of raw materials, concentration of related units, “flow” in manufacture and shipping. Site advantages (water, rail, labor, space). First supplementary to Highland Park, later meant to displace it. Slip, coke ovens, blast furnaces, power house, foundry; Sorensen’s arrival 1921 and control; Rouge River improvement for water transport.
Chapter IX — Projects in Expansion
Lines 9566–10881. Peripheral ideas: timber, iron, silica, coal; glass process; Detroit, Toledo & Ironton Railroad purchase, reconditioning, profit; “village industries” bringing factory to country; Ford fleet; Brazilian rubber adventure; Ford aircraft 1926–1934 as commercial-aviation pioneer. Ford as social and industrial experimenter.
Chapter X — The Greater Company
Lines 10882–12128. Early-1920s organization: research facilities and limits; branch assembly and marketing. Administration and sales under Edsel and E. C. Kanzler; shipment, used cars, price cuts, advertising. Ford’s distrust of formal administration; fluid one-man rule; rise of Liebold (office) and Sorensen (production). Edsel’s difficult position and refusal to oppose his father. Efficiency despite lack of central organization.
Chapter XI — The Rouge: Industrial Colossus
Lines 12129–12953. Rouge’s rising importance versus Highland Park; Sorensen’s drive; mechanization; transfer of units from Highland Park. Experimental steel plant 1923–1926; moving assembly line at Rouge 1927; large-scale discharge of officials. Mature plant: size, modernity, cleanliness; industrial limitations; branch and outside units; essential values surviving later.
Chapter XII — From Muscle Shoals to Anti-Semitism
Lines 12954–13951. Presidential boom 1922–1924; equivocal attitude and final repudiation. Muscle Shoals offer, wide support, Norris opposition, withdrawal. Dearborn Independent anti-Semitic campaign; possible sources of Ford’s attitude; public reaction. Sapiro articles and suit 1924–1927; Ford’s apology to the Jews; harmfulness of the attacks; indulgent public attitude toward Ford’s public-life errors.
Chapter XIII — Labor: A Bright Dawn Pales
Lines 13952–15259. Five-dollar day (1914) and employee-service program; wartime wage effects. Sociological Department standards and activity: investment certificates, liberal employment (Negroes, ex-convicts, handicapped), English and Americanization classes, Ford Trade School, grocery and housing. Dean Marquis’s departure 1921 and end of the idealistic era; retention of some benefits; anti-union attitude and realistic wage policy.
Chapter XIV — Ford Overseas: The Expansive Years
Lines 15260–16335. Model T reputation abroad during and after the war; early-1920s expansion plans; Knudsen’s European survey; Ford and General Motors abroad; Sir Percival Perry and his departure. Plants under Edsel and Sorensen in France, Denmark, Germany, Spain, Italy; prosperous Canadian company work in Australasia and South Africa; Latin American expansion.
Chapter XV — Winds of Challenge
Lines 16336–17536. Early-1920s motor-car effect on American life: highways, motels, buses, truck freight. Model T improvements 1914–1920 and defects; Ford’s resistance to alteration. Competitors—Chevrolet, Overland, Dodge—appearance and comfort versus utility; women’s role in car selection. Price cuts preserve leadership while Chevrolet gains. “X” car as hoped-for T successor; Edsel and Kanzler advocate a new car.
Chapter XVI — The End of Model T
Lines 17537–18628. Kanzler’s January 1926 memorandum proposing a new car; Ford’s hostile response; Kanzler’s departure. Pride, residual T support, hope for a revolutionary successor. Price cuts lose effectiveness; dealer pressure fails; “X” car experiments fail. Hints then announcement of a new model; Model T closes an extraordinary career.
Chapter XVII — Throes of New Birth
Lines 18629–19522. National interest in the unborn car; Ford’s plans; engineers with Laurence Sheldrick as chief designer. Research shortcomings; Ford’s unusual methods. Hicks’s engine work; Model A completed late 1927. Advances over T in design, comfort, appearance; durability and low price; cost in time and money of development.
Chapter XVIII — Model A: A New Era
Lines 19523–20329. Public excitement and order backlog; limping production from quality insistence, unforeseen changes, prior discharges of able officials. Dealer desperation; Universal Credit Corporation for time-payment sales. Chevrolet’s new model; Chrysler’s background, Dodge purchase, Plymouth as cheap car. Model A’s great year 1929.
Chapter XIX — Projects and Personalities
Lines 20330–21529. Fair Lane: Clara’s gardens, Henry’s trees, birds, farm experiments. Edsel at Gaukler Pointe. Friends and camping with Edison, Burroughs, Firestone; Fort Myers winters near the Edisons; Georgia estate beginnings; Edsel’s Seal Harbor and Haven Hill. Diet and health ideas; ban on smoking and drinking; soy beans; old-fashioned dances. Opposition to “philanthropy” and praise of self-help; Henry Ford Hospital, Berry Schools, Greenfield Village; educational contributions.
Chapter XX — How the Workers Fared
Lines 21530–22898. 1920s auto labor: unions not a factor in worker gains. Ford plant goods: cleanliness, light, air, safety, liberal hiring. Contrasts: silence, exact rules, no smoking or chewing; “drive” and conflicting testimony on pace. Five-day week and wage effects; seven-dollar day 1929–1931; low-wage supplier accusation; case for Ford’s policy. Anti-union stance; increasing reliance on Harry Bennett; plant espionage; use of Negro workers.
Chapter XXI — Ford Overseas: The Years of Storm
Lines 22899–24093. 1928 overseas reorganization; Perry’s return supervising European plants; Dagenham on the Thames; sale of British and other Ford companies’ stock. Growing European industrial nationalism hurts France, Germany, Italy; better conditions in Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden, Spain, Britain. German pressure; China impracticable; Japan activity. Depression and nationalism squeeze overseas business.
Chapter XXII — Impact of Depression
Lines 24094–25209. Relative Ford prosperity early in the depression; other firms’ failures. 1931 losses; branch construction, price cuts. Chrysler as competitive factor; gift of a Plymouth to the Fords. Dealer feud over low discounts—dealers win. Workforce sharply reduced; grievances; Bennett’s enlarged power. V-8 planned and introduced March 1932 after Model A; eventual success.
Chapter XXIII — Ford: Symbol, Legend, Reality
Lines 25210–26243. Moving Forward (1931) and Ford’s ideas. Ford as symbol of the mass-production era; appearance, manner, accomplishments. Controversy; popularity in Russia; mixed reception in Ireland, Germany, England, Italy, the United States. Legend fostered by pithy utterance; books by Merz, Marquis, Crowther. Actual Ford: social vision of industrialism’s effects, mechanical genius, faith in experiment; many-faceted personality; rural youth; unhappy attitude toward Edsel. Balance of accomplishments (including associates’) against defects.
Notes, Appendices, Bibliographical Note, and Index
Lines 26244–end. Chapter-keyed notes; appendices including “The Russian Adventure” and related documentary matter; bibliographical note on Ford Archives and related collections; index through final OCR pages. Illustrations list (Rouge diagrams, Liberty engine, Eagle boat, tractor with Northcliffe, Fair Lane, Firestone/Wills/Ford, Coolidge telegram, etc.) appears before the body in the raw extract.
Coverage Guide
War, peace, and public politics
Chapters II, III, V, and XII cover the Peace Ship, war production and the profits pledge, Wilson support and the Newberry race, Tribune trial, Muscle Shoals, and the Dearborn Independent’s anti-Semitic campaign through the Sapiro suit and apology.
Corporate power and organization
Chapters IV, VI, VII, X, and XXIII cover the Dodge suit and minority buy-out, postwar financial crisis and banker defiance, Lincoln acquisition, one-man rule under Liebold and Sorensen, Edsel’s constrained role, and the interpretive balance of symbol, legend, and reality.
Rouge, vertical integration, and experiments
Chapters I, VIII, IX, and XI cover Highland Park’s 1915 showcase, Rouge concept and colossus, raw materials, DT&I railroad, village industries, Brazilian rubber, and aircraft.
Model T to Model A and depression competition
Chapters XV–XVIII and XXII cover competitive challenge, end of Model T, birth and boom of Model A, Chrysler/Plymouth, early depression losses, and the V-8.
Labor
Chapters XIII and XX cover the fading Sociological ideal, Marquis’s exit, five-day and seven-dollar policies, plant discipline, Bennett, espionage, and Negro employment.
Overseas Ford
Chapters XIV and XXI cover expansive interwar planting of factories and the later storm of nationalism, Dagenham, and depression pressure.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 130–200: Preface on 1915–33 forces, Rouge and Model T expansion, Columbia independence, Ford Archives.
Lines 639–720: Panama-Pacific assembly-line exhibit and 1915 world context.
Lines 1655–1720: Schwimmer, Lochner, continuous mediation, and launch of the peace effort.
Lines 2857–2920: Conversion from pacifism to war production behind Wilson.
Lines 4185–4300 region: Dodge suit, dividend, and drive for absolute stock control (open at Drive for Power).
Lines 12954–13200 region: Muscle Shoals and Independent anti-Semitism cluster.
Lines 17537–17650: End of Model T / Kanzler memorandum aftermath.
Lines 19523–19650: Model A public frenzy and production lag.
Lines 21530–21700: Worker conditions, Bennett, and espionage.
Lines 24094–24250: Depression impact and V-8 turn.
Lines 25210–25400: Symbol, legend, reality summation on Ford and Edsel.

Suggested Future Pages

Henry Ford (1915–1933 arc) — entity: Peace Ship, war production, minority buy-out, Independent, Rouge, Model T/A, Bennett.
Edsel Ford — entity: marriage, Lincoln, constrained presidency, design and sales advocacy.
River Rouge Plant — entity/concept: vertical integration, steel, assembly transfer from Highland Park.
Model T (climax and end) — concept/event: 1915–27 career, price cuts, competitive failure, shutdown.
Model A — concept/event: 1927–31 design, Universal Credit, 1929 peak.
Dearborn Independent / Ford anti-Semitism — event/concept: campaign, Sapiro, apology.
Peace Ship (Oscar II) — event: continuous mediation, Schwimmer–Lochner, Norway exit.
Harry Bennett — entity: service department, espionage, rising power in the early 1930s.
Ford overseas (interwar) — concept: Perry, Dagenham, European nationalism, Canada/Latin America.

Related Sources

Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company — Volume I to ~1915–18; five-dollar day, Highland Park origins, Selden, company founding (United States 1866–1919 wiki).
Ford: Decline and Rebirth, 1933–1962 — Volume III: NRA, UAW, Willow Run, Bennett vs. Henry II, Breech, Ford Foundation.
Only Yesterday — contemporary 1920s public mind against which Ford’s celebrity and Independent episode sit.
Since Yesterday — 1929–39 depression and New Deal frame for late chapters and the handoff to Volume III.

Notes on Scope
Columbia-administered, company-archives-rich modern secondary history (1957). Mine as the major narrative bridge for Ford and the American automobile industry from Wilson’s second term through the onset of the Depression and the V-8. Treat Volume II as complete for 1915–1933, not as the full Ford story; labor violence climax, UAW recognition, World War II production, and postwar managerial revolution belong to Volume III. OCR artifacts require caution on exact wording of short quotations; chapter arguments and factual scaffolding are solid.

sources/olcott-life-of-william-mckinley-.title: [source] The Life of William McKinley, Volume II (Olcott, 1916)
sources/olcott-life-of-william-mckinley-.content:
The Life of William McKinley, Volume II
Author: Charles S. Olcott
Published: Houghton Mifflin Company, 1916
Working text: Hathi/Internet Archive-style OCR ZIP via Anna’s Archive (oclc 2690121, hash 2322399fcb8aaf3f8c7896723a957d2f)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/olcott-life-of-william-mckinley.txt (joined OCR page text with page markers)
Extract stats: 472 OCR page files · 16,821 lines · ~104,262 words · 655,045 bytes
Completeness Assessment
The source appears complete as Volume II of a two-volume biography, not as the entire biography. The OCR ZIP sorts naturally from 00000001.txt through 00000472.txt and includes the Volume II title/copyright pages, contents, illustrations list, Chapters XXIV–XXXV, appendix, and index. Blank scan pages and a few OCR artifacts are present, but the contents and back matter run through the end of the volume.
Because this is Volume II, it begins with McKinley’s presidency already underway. It does not contain the earlier chapters on McKinley’s childhood, Civil War service, Ohio politics, congressional career, governorship, tariff politics, or the 1896 election except through index references back to Volume I.
Overview
Olcott’s second volume is a presidency-centered biography of William McKinley from the Cuban crisis through his assassination and memorialization. Its strongest material for this wiki is the transition from continental post-Civil War politics into overseas war and imperial administration: intervention in Cuba, the Spanish-American War, the Treaty of Paris, the Philippines, Cuba and Puerto Rico, China and the Open Door, and McKinley’s reelection in 1900.
The source should be used as a period biography rather than a neutral diplomatic monograph. It is sympathetic to McKinley, often defending his caution, judgment, and administrative balance. That makes it valuable for contemporary and near-contemporary pro-McKinley framing, especially when paired with The House of Morgan for finance and empire-era diplomacy, Andrew Carnegie for anti-imperial and public moral context, Titan for late-Gilded-Age Republican political economy, and Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company for the industrial and international-commercial world into which McKinley’s final Buffalo speech looked forward.
Narrative Source Flow
Front Matter and Illustrations
Lines 19–171. The front matter identifies this as Volume II of Olcott’s biography and provides a contents list from Chapter XXIV through Chapter XXXV. The illustrations center the public presidency: McKinley at Buffalo, the peace protocol, a memorandum on Dewey and the Philippines, the cabinet, military figures, the 1900 acceptance speech, Ida Saxton McKinley, Canton, and memorial sites.
Chapter XXIV — Intervention
Lines 187–1166. The volume opens with the pressures that pushed the United States toward intervention in Cuba: sympathy for Cuban suffering, sanitary fears, trade and investment losses, hazards to American residents, neutrality enforcement, and doubts that Spain could end the war. Olcott emphasizes McKinley’s reluctance to rush into war, his interest in giving Spain’s Sagasta ministry time, and his movement toward forcible intervention only after diplomacy and autonomy schemes failed.
Chapter XXV — The Spanish-American War
Lines 1167–1994. This chapter covers congressional resolutions, war authority, the Teller Amendment, the opening of hostilities, strategy, naval and military preparations, Dewey’s orders and victory at Manila, operations around Cuba, and the American war effort. It presents McKinley as coordinating reluctant but increasingly decisive war policy from Washington.
Chapter XXVI — The End of the War
Lines 1995–2654. Olcott follows the closing stage of the war after Santiago: Spanish capitulation, peace feelers, the protocol, occupation questions, and the rapid collapse of Spain’s military position. The chapter is useful for tracing how battlefield success translated into diplomatic bargaining and administrative burdens.
Chapter XXVII — A Wave of Criticism
Lines 2655–3212. The war’s military success is followed by criticism of army administration, camp conditions, disease, supply failures, and public controversy. Olcott treats the controversy as a test of wartime organization and presidential responsibility, making this chapter a useful source for the limits of late-nineteenth-century federal military administration.
Chapter XXVIII — The Peace Negotiations
Lines 3213–4875. McKinley appoints William R. Day, Cushman K. Davis, William P. Frye, George Gray, and Whitelaw Reid as peace commissioners. The chapter tracks the Paris negotiations, the central question of the Philippines, relations with European powers, the changing attitude of Britain, and the Senate fight over ratification.
Chapter XXIX — The Making of the Philippines
Lines 4876–6615. Olcott moves from the Spanish colonial crisis into American Philippine policy. The chapter covers revolt, Aguinaldo, Dewey, Manila, instructions and commissions, the problem of sovereignty, native government, insurrection, and McKinley’s reasoning about American responsibility in the islands.
Chapter XXX — The New Government in the Antilles
Lines 6616–7506. This chapter covers Cuba and Puerto Rico after the Treaty of Paris. It follows military occupation, obligations assumed by the United States, the Foraker Act and Puerto Rican tariff issues, constitutional questions, and the practical problem of converting wartime occupation into civil administration.
Chapter XXXI — China
Lines 7507–8899. The chapter treats the China crisis and Open Door policy during McKinley’s presidency. It covers John Hay’s illness and policy role, Boxer violence, protection of the legations, instructions to General Chaffee, the American effort to preserve Chinese territorial integrity, and the final settlement that kept the Open Door from becoming formal partition.
Chapter XXXII — Renomination and Reelection
Lines 8900–10467. Olcott places the 1900 election in the changed national mood after prosperity, war victory, and imperial debate. The chapter follows the Republican renomination, vice-presidential politics, Theodore Roosevelt’s nomination, Bryan and Democratic opposition, free silver and imperialism, front-porch campaigning, and McKinley’s reelection.
Chapter XXXIII — Looking Forward
Lines 10468–11062. The second inaugural and early second term are treated as a moment of enlarged national confidence. Olcott emphasizes McKinley’s changed stature after four years in office, his search for conciliation, and his forward-looking program of prosperity, reciprocity, international trade, peace, and national responsibility.
Chapter XXXIV — The Tragedy at Buffalo
Lines 11063–11738. This chapter narrates McKinley’s visit to the Pan-American Exposition, the public reception at Buffalo, Leon Czolgosz’s attack, the medical crisis, public anxiety, the president’s death, and the emotional national response. It is the principal source section for the assassination and transition to mourning.
Chapter XXXV — Conclusion
Lines 11739–13142. Olcott closes with an explicit appraisal of McKinley’s character, leadership, public virtues, and place in national memory. The conclusion is strongly commemorative and should be used as evidence of the post-assassination McKinley memorial tradition as much as of the presidency itself.
Appendix and Index
Lines 13143–16821. The appendix preserves McKinley’s last public address at Buffalo on September 5, 1901, including his statements on expositions, international commerce, modern communications, prosperity, foreign markets, reciprocity, and the impossibility of isolation. The index runs through the end of the OCR and is especially useful because it points back to Volume I entries as well as Volume II subjects.
Coverage Guide
Spanish-American War and Intervention
Chapters XXIV–XXVI form the intervention and war core: Cuba, Spain, Congress, naval preparedness, Dewey, Santiago, protocol, and the shift from humanitarian and commercial concern to formal war. These sections should feed future pages on the Spanish-American War, Cuban intervention, Teller Amendment, and McKinley’s war leadership.
Empire, Islands, and Constitutional Questions
Chapters XXVIII–XXX cover the postwar settlement: Treaty of Paris, Philippines, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Foraker Act, occupation, civil government, and constitutional uncertainty about new possessions. These chapters support future pages on American empire, Philippine-American War context, Puerto Rico, Cuba under U.S. occupation, and the Insular Cases background.
China and Open Door Diplomacy
Chapter XXXI is the China-policy core. It gives a presidency-centered account of the Boxer crisis, legation danger, John Hay’s Open Door diplomacy, Chaffee’s expedition, and the American effort to preserve Chinese integrity without partition.
Election of 1900 and Republican Politics
Chapter XXXII links prosperity, imperialism, Bryan, Roosevelt, Republican confidence, and McKinley’s reelection. It should feed future pages on the election of 1900, Republican Party politics, Bryan’s anti-imperial campaign, and Roosevelt’s move toward national power.
McKinley’s Final Public Program
Chapter XXXIII and the appendix are especially valuable for McKinley’s late program: reciprocity, trade outlets, modern transportation and communications, arbitration, prosperity, and the claim that isolation was no longer possible or desirable.
Assassination and Memorialization
Chapters XXXIV–XXXV and the illustrations capture the assassination at Buffalo, Ida Saxton McKinley, public mourning, Canton memorial culture, and the commemorative presentation of McKinley as soldier, executive, unifier, and moral exemplar.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 187–360: reasons for intervention in Cuba and McKinley’s argument for giving Spain’s new ministry a chance before war.
Lines 1167–1994: congressional war resolutions, Teller Amendment setting, Dewey, Cuba operations, and early war administration.
Lines 3213–4875: Paris peace commissioners, Philippines debate, European powers, Britain, and treaty ratification.
Lines 4876–6615: Philippine policy, Aguinaldo, Manila, American sovereignty, commissions, and the logic of imperial responsibility.
Lines 6616–7506: Cuba and Puerto Rico administration, Foraker Act, tariffs, and constitutional questions.
Lines 7507–8899: Boxer crisis, John Hay, Open Door policy, Chaffee, legations, and Chinese settlement.
Lines 8900–10467: 1900 election, Roosevelt vice-presidential nomination, Bryan, prosperity, silver, and imperialism.
Lines 11063–11738: Buffalo assassination narrative and national reaction.
Lines 13143–13885: McKinley’s last public address on commerce, progress, communications, foreign markets, reciprocity, and the end of isolation.

Suggested Future Pages

William McKinley — entity page on presidency, tariff politics, war leadership, imperial settlement, assassination, and public memory.
Spanish-American War — event page on causes, congressional authorization, naval operations, Cuba, Manila, Santiago, and peace protocol.
Treaty of Paris 1898 — event/concept page on cession, indemnity, Senate ratification, and anti-imperial controversy.
Philippine-American War / Philippine Policy — event/concept page on Aguinaldo, sovereignty, commissions, civil government, and American imperial responsibility.
Open Door Policy — concept page on China, John Hay, Boxer crisis, legation rescue, and U.S. anti-partition diplomacy.
Election of 1900 — event page on McKinley, Bryan, Roosevelt, prosperity, imperialism, and free silver.
Assassination of William McKinley — event page on Buffalo, Czolgosz, death, succession, and memorial culture.
Reciprocity and International Trade — concept page centered on McKinley’s final address and the turn from high tariff confidence toward reciprocal trade arrangements.

Related Sources

The House of Morgan — finance, diplomacy, overseas investment, and the broader imperial-financial world of McKinley’s presidency.
Andrew Carnegie — anti-imperial politics, peace advocacy, public morality, and elite reactions to empire and war.
Titan — Republican-era political economy, philanthropy, public reputation, and corporate wealth in the McKinley period.
Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company — industrial prosperity, modern communications, export markets, and the commercial future McKinley described in his last speech.
The Wizard of Menlo Park — technological modernity, public celebrity, and the electrical/communications world underlying late McKinley-era public life.

Notes on Scope
This source is a sympathetic 1916 biography, close enough to McKinley’s generation to preserve commemorative language and administration-friendly interpretation. It should be mined for McKinley-era narrative, speeches, and policy framing, while later synthetic pages should balance it against other sources where possible.

sources/paxson-recent-history-united-sta.title: [source] Recent History of the United States, 1865–1927 (Paxson, 1928/1929)
sources/paxson-recent-history-united-sta.content:
Recent History of the United States, 1865–1927
Author: Frederic L. Paxson
Published: Houghton Mifflin, revised and enlarged edition, copyright 1928/1929
Working text: Hathi/IA-style OCR ZIP via Anna’s Archive (oclc 816137, hash c9f117629c6ba1aee0f51a53dc7e84da)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/paxson-recent-history-united-states-1865-1927.txt
Extract stats: 712 OCR page files · 32,026 lines · ~253,868 words · 1,571,589 bytes
Completeness Assessment
The OCR ZIP appears complete as a single-volume revised and enlarged edition. The joined raw text includes title/copyright pages, preface, full contents, list of maps, Chapters I–XXVII, and index. The title page gives the scope as 1865–1927, although the file name says 1865–1929; the text should therefore be treated as Paxson’s 1865–1927 narrative in a 1928/1929 printing.
Overview
Paxson describes the United States after the Civil War as a transition from agricultural civilization to industrial society, from isolation to world eminence, and from European debtor to international creditor and power. The book is an especially useful backbone source because it connects the whole period of this wiki: Reconstruction, the railroad and frontier economy, money and tariff politics, Populism, the 1890s crisis, McKinley, Spanish-American War, Roosevelt, Progressive regulation, Wilson, World War I, the peace settlement, and the first postwar political settlement.
For this wiki, its strongest value is the 1900–1919 narrative core: Roosevelt, imperialism, trusts, muckraking, federal control, Taft, insurgency, Wilson, neutrality, preparedness, World War I, the American war government, peace, and the League. It pairs with The Life of William McKinley, Volume II for McKinley-era diplomacy, Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company for industrial mass production, The House of Morgan for finance and world power, and Andrew Carnegie for anti-imperial and peace politics.
Narrative Source Flow
Preface and Framing
Lines 58–79. Paxson frames the book as a history of a new industrial, post-frontier, world-facing United States. The stated theme is not merely political chronology but the structural transformation of American society after the Civil War.
Chapters I–IV — Union, Reconstruction, Readjustment, and Postwar Politics
Lines 770–4862. These chapters cover the control of the Union, Reconstruction, the Fourteenth Amendment, Johnson, Grant, the Far West, railroads, Indian wars, greenbacks, panic, Liberal Republicans, education, literature, postwar thought, Hayes, Garfield, Arthur, patronage, strikes, labor, and factional Republican politics.
Chapters V–VIII — Material Basis, Cleveland, Frontier Aftermath, and Protection
Lines 4863–9308. Paxson turns to economic realities: silver, specie resumption, railroads, Standard Oil, inventions, New South, tariff reform, Cleveland, public lands, cattle, Interstate Commerce, sport, urbanization, labor parties, ballot reform, Harrison, the McKinley tariff, silver legislation, pensions, and the Sherman Anti-Trust Act.
Chapters IX–XII — Farmers’ West, Panic, Gold Standard, and War with Spain
