Lines 9309–13808. This cluster covers Populism, statehood, free silver, the Panic of 1893, Homestead, Debs, Cleveland’s bond issues, the Wilson tariff, Venezuela, the new navy, McKinley, Hanna, Bryan, gold, the Dingley tariff, Cuba, yellow journalism, the Maine, Manila, Santiago, Hawaii, the Philippines, and Theodore Roosevelt’s rise.
Chapter XIII — The Age of Roosevelt
Lines 13809–14564. Paxson opens the twentieth-century section with McKinley, the Currency Act of 1900, prosperity, trusts, the 1900 campaign, imperialism, McKinley’s assassination, Theodore Roosevelt’s presidency, political reform, letters and sport, Booker T. Washington, labor unrest, and the enlarged presidential office.
Chapter XIV — The New Imperialism
Lines 14565–15482. The chapter treats Roosevelt, Hay, Root, Panama, the Hay-Pauncefote and Hay-Herrán treaties, the Panama secession, Goethals, Venezuela, the Monroe Doctrine, Puerto Rico, Cuba, the Philippines, War Department reorganization, the General Staff, the fleet’s world cruise, Portsmouth, Algeciras, the Hague, and the Declaration of London.
Chapters XV–XVII — Business, Muckraking, and Federal Control
Lines 15483–17542. Paxson follows railroads, mergers, United States Steel, Northern Securities, antitrust legislation, the Department of Commerce and Labor, Cuban reciprocity, the anthracite strike, campaign contributions, muckraking, Ida Tarbell, new journalism, universities, expert government, immigration, the Hepburn law, Pure Food Act, Roosevelt Panic of 1907, Aldrich-Vreeland Act, and conservation.
Chapters XVIII–XX — Taft, Insurgency, and Wilson
Lines 17543–20728. These chapters cover Taft’s election and cabinet, Payne-Aldrich tariff, income tax amendment, insurgent Republicans, Ballinger, Cannon, direct election of senators, postal savings, Panama Canal, Canadian reciprocity, arbitration treaties, Carnegie and peace, Roosevelt’s return, New Nationalism, the Progressive Party, Wilson’s election, tariff revision, Federal Reserve, Federal Trade Commission, labor legislation, the Philippines, woman suffrage, socialism, syndicalism, and the I.W.W.
Chapters XXI–XXIV — Neutrality, World War I, War Government, and Peace
Lines 20729–26206. Paxson covers Bryan, Mexico, Vera Cruz, canal diplomacy, Caribbean policy, neutrality, propaganda, submarine warfare, Lusitania, preparedness, the 1916 election, the German peace overture, unrestricted submarine warfare, the war session of Congress, Council of National Defense, Committee on Public Information, Hoover, munitions, finance, selective service, Pershing and the A.E.F., War Trade Board, Alien Property Custodian, Food and Fuel control, War Industries Board, labor policy, Fourteen Points, the 1918 battles, armistice, Wilson in Europe, the Big Four, League covenant, American Legion, and economic demobilization.
Chapters XXV–XXVII — Postwar Environment and Normalcy
Lines 26207–29757. The final chapters move beyond this wiki’s endpoint into postwar society, aviation, wireless, motor cars, highways, movies, Prohibition, Ku Klux Klan, fundamentalism, Versailles, Wilson’s collapse, strikes of 1919, radicalism, woman suffrage, railroad legislation, Harding, Coolidge, immigration restriction, foreign debts, World Court, Panama, Nicaragua, Mexico, China, naval limitation, and the politics of the 1920s.
Index
Lines 29758–32026. The index is extensive and useful for locating names and subjects across the full 1865–1927 narrative.
Coverage Guide
The book should be mined first as the period’s synthetic spine. Chapters I–XII support Reconstruction, Gilded Age politics, economic change, Populism, the 1890s, McKinley, and the Spanish-American War. Chapters XIII–XXIV are the strongest fit for 1900–1919: Roosevelt, Progressivism, empire, trust regulation, Taft, Wilson, neutrality, war mobilization, and peace. Chapters XXV–XXVII should be used selectively for immediate postwar spillover, especially 1919 strikes, demobilization, normalcy politics, and the postwar social environment.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 58–79: Paxson’s thesis on industrial society, world eminence, and the post-frontier United States.
Lines 13809–15482: McKinley/Roosevelt transition and the New Imperialism.
Lines 15483–17542: trusts, business politics, muckraking, federal regulation, and conservation.
Lines 17543–20728: Taft, insurgency, Progressive Party, Wilson’s domestic program, and labor/social reform.
Lines 20729–26206: neutrality, preparedness, World War I, war government, armistice, peace, and League of Nations.
Lines 26207–27207: postwar society, Prohibition, Klan, motor cars, roads, communications, and cultural change.

Suggested Future Pages

Progressive Era — concept page linking Roosevelt, Taft, Wilson, regulation, muckraking, conservation, and labor.
New Imperialism — concept/event cluster on Panama, Caribbean, Philippines, Roosevelt diplomacy, and naval power.
World War I Mobilization in the United States — concept page on war boards, finance, food, fuel, labor, and selective service.
Election of 1912 — event page on Taft, Roosevelt, Wilson, New Nationalism, and Progressive Party.
