sources/wall-andrew-carnegie.content:
Andrew Carnegie
Author: Joseph Frazier Wall
Published: University of Pittsburgh Press, 1989 second edition; originally Oxford University Press, 1970
Working text: Internet Archive PDF via Anna’s Archive (isbn13 9780822938286, hash c53a3540e6caceaf3d42813fd4d83770)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/wall-andrew-carnegie.txt (pdftotext -layout from PDF)
Extract stats: 58,209 lines · ~468,432 words · 3,203,692 bytes · 1,172 PDF pages
Overview
Wall’s Andrew Carnegie is a full-scale biography of Carnegie from Dunfermline childhood through immigration, Pittsburgh telegraph and railroad work, Civil War opportunities, diversified investment, bridge and iron ventures, the rise of Carnegie Steel, the Homestead crisis, sale to United States Steel, and the long philanthropic and peace-seeking afterlife of his fortune. The book is organized in three broad movements: The Charter (origins and migration), The Contract (business career, 1853–1901), and The Deed (philanthropy, empire of giving, peace, and final years, 1899–1919).
For this United States 1866–1919 wiki, the source is central for industrial capitalism, steel, Pittsburgh, railroad-linked entrepreneurship, labor conflict, philanthropy, anti-imperial politics, elite transatlantic networks, libraries, higher education, peace activism, and the moral self-fashioning of a Gilded Age capitalist. It pairs naturally with Titan for oil/steel comparisons, with A Life of George Westinghouse for Pittsburgh industrial technology, and with The Wizard of Menlo Park for fame, invention, and public reputation.
The raw text is usable but noisy in the scanned contents pages: chapter headings and body text are mostly readable, while some table-of-contents lines are garbled by OCR. Chapter body starts are clear enough for mining.
Narrative Source Flow
Preface to the Second Edition / Preface / Acknowledgments
Lines 212–430. Wall’s retrospective note on the 1989 edition, relationship to earlier Carnegie scholarship, acknowledgments, and research framing.
Chapter I — Prologue: Dunfermline, 1835
Lines 444–1036. Dunfermline setting, British industrial and social background, Scottish civic culture, and the world into which Carnegie was born.
Chapter II — The Inheritance, 1740–1835
Lines 1037–2066. Carnegie family background, Morrison and Carnegie lines, religious/political inheritance, Chartism, radicalism, and household traditions before Andrew’s birth.
Chapter III — Childhood, 1835–1848
Lines 2067–3314. Dunfermline childhood, handloom weaving, family hardship, schooling, politics, memory, and the pressures leading toward emigration.
Chapter IV — The Flitting, 1848
Lines 3315–4249. Decision to leave Scotland, transatlantic migration, arrival in America, and the social meaning of the family’s move.
Chapter V — Charter Acquired, 1848–1855
Lines 4250–5787. Early Pittsburgh and Allegheny years, work, education, telegraphy, family advancement, and Carnegie’s acquisition of skills and ambitions.
Chapter VI — Mr. Scott’s Andy, 1853–1859
Lines 5788–7404. Pennsylvania Railroad apprenticeship under Thomas A. Scott, telegraph/railroad management, advancement, investments, and patronage.
Chapter VII — War and Profits of War, 1860–1865
Lines 7405–9698. Civil War service, Scott and federal transport, wartime contracts, railroads, bridges, oil, telegraphy, and Carnegie’s rising capital.
Chapter VIII — Many Eggs, Many Baskets, 1865–1874
Lines 9699–11451. Postwar diversified investments, Pullman/sleeping cars, bonds, railroads, oil, and Carnegie’s habit of spreading risks.
Chapter IX — A Basket of Iron, 1865–1872
Lines 11452–13441. Iron manufacture, Keystone Bridge, Pittsburgh industrial opportunities, and Carnegie’s move toward metallurgical enterprise.
Chapter X — Bridges and Bonds, 1868–1872
Lines 13442–15406. Bridge building, bond sales, capital formation, European finance, and the business networks supporting Carnegie’s manufacturing ventures.
Chapter XI — Steel Is King, 1873–1881
Lines 15407–18146. Bessemer steel, Edgar Thomson works, depression-era opportunity, cost discipline, plant building, and the emergence of Carnegie steel.
Chapter XII — Unnatural Selection, 1878–1887
Lines 18147–20001. Competitive struggle, business selection, consolidation, managerial choices, and Carnegie’s sharpening industrial methods.
Chapter XIII — Courtship and Marriage, 1880–1887
Lines 20002–21145. Family and domestic life, relationship with Louise Whitfield, Margaret Carnegie, and Carnegie’s delayed marriage.
Chapter XIV — The Two Worlds of Andrew Carnegie, 1881–1896
Lines 21146–23586. Carnegie’s transatlantic life, literary/social ambitions, public causes, business absenteeism, and divided identity between culture and industry.
Chapter XV — Enter Mr. Frick, 1881–1892
Lines 23587–26817. Henry Clay Frick, coke, reorganization, Carnegie Steel management, labor policy, and the business structure before Homestead.
Chapter XVI — Homestead, 1892
Lines 26818–29070. Formation of Carnegie Steel, wage conflict, Frick’s lockout, Pinkertons, violence, public reaction, and Carnegie’s distance from events.
Chapter XVII — Mr. Carnegie’s Empire of Business, 1892–1900
Lines 29071–33725. Post-Homestead consolidation, steel expansion, vertical integration, profits, rivals, and Carnegie Steel’s place in American industry.
Chapter XVIII — Mr. McKinley’s Business of Empire, 1898–1900
Lines 33726–35972. Spanish-American War era politics, anti-imperialism, McKinley, business empire, and Carnegie’s public-political interventions.
Chapter XIX — Exit Mr. Frick, 1899–1900
Lines 35973–38623. Carnegie-Frick break, lawsuits, personal/business conflict, and unraveling of their partnership.
Chapter XX — The Contract Closed
Lines 38624–40124. Sale negotiations, J. P. Morgan, creation of United States Steel, Carnegie’s retirement from business, and conversion of steel holdings into bonds.
Chapter XXI — The Gospel of Wealth, 1889–1901
Lines 40125–40772. Carnegie’s doctrine of wealth, early organized giving, libraries, pensions, and first large acts after business retirement.
Chapter XXII — Philanthropy Becomes Big Business, 1901–1911
Lines 40773–44692. Carnegie libraries, church organs, Scottish universities, Dunfermline, Carnegie Institute, Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching, institutionalized giving, and educational reform.
Chapter XXIII — The Quest for Peace, 1901–1910
Lines 44693–47686. Peace societies, arbitration, international law, Hague ideals, public advocacy, and Carnegie’s use of philanthropy for peace.
Chapter XXIV — Sunshine at Skibo, 1901–1914
Lines 47687–51840. Skibo Castle, family and leisure, elite networks, guests, rituals, and the private world of Carnegie’s later years.
Chapter XXV — Shadows at Shadowbrook, 1914–1919
Lines 51841–52216. World War I, disappointment in peace hopes, declining health, Shadowbrook, final years, and death.
Epilogue — The Deed Continues, 1919–
Lines 51957–52216. Carnegie legacy and continuation of his philanthropic deed after death; overlaps in OCR with final-chapter end and transition into notes.
Notes / Index
Lines 52217–58209. Chapter notes and index, including source trails for correspondence, business records, institutions, public controversies, and later scholarship.
Coverage Guide
Carnegie, steel, and post-Civil War capitalism
Chapters VI–XX are the core business arc. They show Carnegie’s rise through Pennsylvania Railroad patronage, Civil War logistical opportunities, postwar investment, iron bridges, bonds, Bessemer steel, Edgar Thomson, Carnegie Steel, Frick, Homestead, vertical integration, and sale to United States Steel. This is the steel counterpart to Rockefeller’s oil empire in Titan.
Labor conflict and Homestead
Chapters XV and XVI are the key sections for a future Homestead event page. They connect Frick, coke, wage conflict, lockout, Pinkertons, violence, public opinion, and Carnegie’s own absentee responsibility. Chapter XVII then shows how Carnegie Steel expanded after the crisis.
Philanthropy and the Gospel of Wealth
Chapters XXI–XXIII are the strongest material for Carnegie’s public doctrine and institutional giving: free libraries, church organs, Scottish universities, Dunfermline, Carnegie Institute, Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching, and peace projects. This material complements Rockefeller philanthropy in Titan, but Carnegie’s giving is more explicitly tied to his published moral theory of surplus wealth.
Pittsburgh and industrial technology
Carnegie’s Pittsburgh, railroad, bridge, iron, steel, and finance career pairs with A Life of George Westinghouse, another Pittsburgh-centered industrial biography. Together they can support pages on Pittsburgh industry, rail-connected entrepreneurship, steel/electrical infrastructure, and the city’s role in Gilded Age industrial systems.
Public persona, writing, and transatlantic networks
Chapters XIV, XVIII, XXIII, and XXIV are useful for Carnegie’s two-world life: industrialist and man of letters, Scot and American, businessman and public moralist, anti-imperialist and peace advocate, Skibo host and global celebrity. This public persona can be compared with Edison’s technological celebrity in The Wizard of Menlo Park.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 4250–7404: early Pittsburgh work, telegraphy, Pennsylvania Railroad, Thomas A. Scott, and the origins of Carnegie’s business habits.
Lines 7405–9698: Civil War logistics, wartime profits, and connections among railroads, telegraphy, oil, and government service.
Lines 11452–18146: iron, bridges, bonds, Bessemer steel, Edgar Thomson, and the transition from diversified capitalism to steel dominance.
Lines 23587–29070: Frick, Carnegie Steel reorganization, labor policy, and Homestead.
Lines 29071–40124: Carnegie Steel’s post-Homestead expansion, empire of business, politics of empire, Frick break, and Morgan/U.S. Steel sale.
Lines 40125–44692: Gospel of Wealth, libraries, Scottish universities, Dunfermline, and philanthropy as institutional business.
Lines 44693–47686: Carnegie’s peace activism, arbitration, and prewar internationalism.
Lines 47687–52216: Skibo, late life, World War I disillusionment, Shadowbrook, death, and legacy.
Lines 52217–58209: notes and index for tracing letters, institutional records, business controversies, and bibliographic leads.

Suggested Future Pages

Andrew Carnegie — entity page on immigrant origins, railroad apprenticeship, steel empire, philanthropy, peace activism, and 1919 death.
Carnegie Steel Company — entity page on Edgar Thomson, vertical integration, Frick, profits, labor policy, and sale to U.S. Steel.
Homestead Strike — event page on 1892 conflict, Pinkertons, workers, Frick, Carnegie, and public reaction.
Gospel of Wealth — concept page on Carnegie’s doctrine of surplus wealth and duties of the millionaire.
Carnegie Libraries — concept/entity page on library giving as mass philanthropy and civic infrastructure.
United States Steel Formation — event/concept page on J. P. Morgan, Carnegie’s sale, and the shift from entrepreneurial steel empire to corporate consolidation.
Carnegie Peace Philanthropy — concept page on arbitration, peace societies, international law, and the limits exposed by World War I.

Related Sources


Titan — oil trust, antitrust politics, philanthropy, and Rockefeller as Carnegie’s peer/rival in wealth and public reputation.


The House of Morgan — Morgan finance, U.S. Steel formation, panic management, and the banking layer behind Carnegie’s steel empire.


A Life of George Westinghouse — Pittsburgh industrial technology, railways, electrical systems, finance, and engineer-industrialist comparison.


The Wizard of Menlo Park — public fame and industrial modernity from the inventor-celebrity side of the Gilded Age.


Ford: The Times, the Man, the Company — automobile mass production and Ford labor policy beside Carnegie steel, Homestead, and large-scale industrial organization.


The Life of William McKinley, Volume II — Spanish-American War, anti-imperial debate, peace rhetoric, and McKinley-era public politics alongside Carnegie’s later activism.


Notes on Scope
This is a modern scholarly biography, not a period memoir. It is nevertheless dense with letters, business history, public controversy, institutional philanthropy, and political context. Its post-1919 material should be treated as legacy and continuation of Carnegie’s institutions rather than as core chronological evidence for the 1866–1919 wiki.
